after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Washington
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.title: Preprint: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
after.authors: Wu, Y.; Asvadi, S.; van der Ven, M.; Peri, E.; Xu, M.; van der Hout-van der Jagt, M. B.; OEH van Laar, J.; Chen, C.; Luo, Q.; Mischi, M.; Oei, S. G.; Long, X.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Eindhoven University of Technology
after.abstract: Risk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. This secondary analysis included 9289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-2013). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported 'no' (low risk), 'yes' (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. The adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each woman's three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). For fetal growth outcomes, how a woman's predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a woman's follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit.

after.title: Preprint: Microcirculation Mirror: A zero-install browser workstation for hand microvascular anatomy and nailfold capillaroscopy
after.authors: Wang, Y.; He, J.; Liu, W.; Xu, X.; Li, B.; Li, Y.; Wang, B.; Liu, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College
after.abstract: Background Hand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 m lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange. Methods We present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module. The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app. Results Its 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer. The NVC module renders a 200x, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification. A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-m capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-m detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains {approx}0.016% effective contrast, about 60x below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is {approx}270x lower. The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6. Conclusions The camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled. No patient data are used. The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.

after.title: Preprint: Requirements of a knowledge support tool for self-harm in general practice: a mixed-methods study with patients, carers, and clinicians
after.authors: Cant, H.; Mughal, F.; Asmal, S.; Petersen, K.; Groves, J.; Gardiner, E.; Bower, P.; Webb, R. T.; Kapur, N.; Westhead, J.; Palin, V.; Pate, A.; van Staa, T.; Quinlivan, L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Manchester
after.abstract: Background General practice has a central role in care following self-harm. However, clinicians frequently report uncertainty about best practice and patients describe poor care. A knowledge support tool is an add-on to electronic health systems that may improve services by providing personalised care information. Aim To understand what general practice clinicians, patients and carers need from a novel knowledge support tool for self-harm. Design and Setting Mixed-methods, using quantitative ratings, focus groups and follow-on interviews with general practice clinicians and patients/carers with lived experience of self-harm. Method Clinicians were recruited through social media and professional networks, and patients/carers through a third-sector organisation. During four focus groups and follow-on interviews, we explored the utility of potential content and functionality of a knowledge support tool. Quantitative utility ratings were summarised descriptively and qualitative data were analysed thematically using the framework method. People with lived/living experience were involved throughout. Results 13 clinicians and 14 patients/carers participated. Requirements of the knowledge support tool were captured across three qualitative themes: facilitating person-centred care, accessibility and usability, and balancing competing priorities of general practice. Across these themes, patients' and carers' needs were centred on promoting compassionate relationships and patient agency. Clinicians shared these needs but balanced them with a need to manage patient expectations and practice defensively under limited resources. Conclusion Our findings inform the core design of a knowledge support tool and suggest that such a tool could support the assessment and management of self-harm in general practice.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Superior Tecnico - Universidade de Lisboa
after.abstract: The gaze direction of the physician during consultations plays an important role in patient satisfaction, with several studies pointing to the positive correlation between the amount of time the physician spends looking at the patient and patient satisfaction. Additionally, the effects of the virtual consultation environment on the gaze behaviour of the doctor have yet to be studied. Therefore, this study aims to assess the impact of the virtual consultation environment by comparing the amount of total time the doctor spends looking at the patient between face-to-face and virtual consultations, as well as the average duration during the consultation and the gaze frequency. The study population consisted of 14 doctors divided between 4 medical specialties: Gynaecology/Obstetrics (4), Neurology (3), Endocrinology (3) and General and Familiar Medicine (4). A low-cost desktop that runs an appearance-based gaze estimation pipeline was implemented in the clinical setup. Each doctor recorded 20 face-to-face consultations and 20 virtual consultations, which were then processed by the pipeline to obtain the percentage of time the doctor spent looking at the patient during the consultation. Overall, we found that doctors look more at the patient in virtual consultations compared to face-to-face consultations, both in total time and average duration during the consultation. Within medical specialties, three out the four specialties involved presented clear tendencies to look more at the patient in virtual consultations when compared to face-to-face consultations.

after.authors: Atiyah, A.; Lamb, B.; Soukup, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Barts Health NHS Trust
after.abstract: Abstract Background: Multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings are central to cancer care. National policy, including the 2026 National Cancer Plan for England, expects MDTs to improve how they work. Although validated tools assess MDT performance, little is known about training in their use. We evaluated structured MDT improvement training delivered across two UK Cancer Alliances. Methods: Three one day courses, delivered in 2019, combined teaching and simulation using MDT assessment tools, including the Metric for the Observation of Decision-making (MDT MODe). Participants completed a 14 item Likert-scale survey (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) and open ended questions. Responses were summarised descriptively; subgroup comparisons used chi squared tests with Bonferroni correction. Free text responses were analysed thematically by two coders. Results: Forty eight MDT members responded (26 doctors, 10 nurses, 10 administrative staff). Twelve of 14 items scored a median of 4 (agree); understanding the information scored a 4.5. Support for mandatory training was more modest (median 3.5). After Bonferroni correction, significant differences by grade remained for knowledge of the MDT metric (adjusted p = 0.001) and MDT MODe instrument (adjusted p < 0.001). Strengths included teaching (n = 14), utility of MDT MODe (n = 10) and networking (n = 9). Weaknesses included poor audio visual quality (n = 18) and difficulty identifying speakers (n = 8). Conclusions: Expert led, simulation-based MDT improvement training was well received across professional groups. Although delivered in 2019, it addresses skills central to national MDT reform. Future courses should improve audio visual quality and offer implementation support. Pre, post evaluation and longer-term follow-up are needed.

after.title: Preprint: Uptake and outcomes of earlier viral load testing and longer visit intervals in the early HIV treatment period: retrospective cohort analysis of South Africas 2023 ART guidelines revision
after.authors: Kachingwe, E.; Maskew, M.; Mutanda, N.; Benade, M.; Scott, N.; Morgan, A.; Sande, L.; Ntjikelane, V.; Malala, L.; Manganyane, M.; Rosen, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: School of Public Health, Boston University, Boston, MA, USA
after.abstract: Background: South Africas 2023 revised ART Guidelines moved the first scheduled viral load (VL) test from 6 to 3 months after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and accelerated differentiated care eligibility from 7 to 4 months among virally suppressed clients. We assessed uptake of these changes and their association with virologic outcomes. Methods: We analysed routine electronic medical record data from 18 primary healthcare clinics in three South African districts among all adults initiating or re-initiating ART (N=16,338; January 2022-March 2025). Interrupted time series analyses were used to assess uptake of 3-month VL testing and assignment to greater than or equal to 6-month visit intervals following guideline implementation in April 2023. Modified Poisson regression was used to compare relative risks (RRs) for viral suppression at the first and second routine VL tests among clients tested at 3 months (test window=56-111 days) and 6 months (112-<252 days). Results: At the first VL assessment, 27% of participants had VL tests at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; the rest had tests outside either window (19%) or no test documented (25%). Three-month VL testing rose immediately after guideline implementation, reaching 72-85% coverage by the end of the study period. Assignment to greater than or equal to 6month visit intervals among clients with 3-month viral suppression increased after implementation, reaching 48-71% across districts. A second VL result was documented for 62% of clients tested in the 3- or 6-month window. Viral suppression did not differ meaningfully between clients initially tested at 3 months (72%) and those initially tested at 6 months (72%). Among clients with a second scheduled VL result, 82% were virally suppressed. Assignment to greater than or equal to 6-month visit intervals was not associated with subsequent viral suppression (aRR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.06). Results should be interpreted with caution due to missing VL data. Conclusion: South Africas 2023 guideline revision was associated with rapid increases in 3-month VL testing and assignment to longer visit intervals. Viral suppression at the first VL test was similar among clients tested at 3 and 6 months, and longer visit intervals were not associated with poorer outcomes. These findings support earlier differentiation of HIV care within routine service delivery. Incomplete uptake of recommended testing and visit intervals offers opportunities to strengthen implementation and warrants continued evaluation of longer-term outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Practical evaluation of AI models to forecast a respiratory seasonal epidemic in Canada
after.authors: Benteke, B. L.; Yusuf, W.; Cojocaru, M. G.; Champredon, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Guelph
after.abstract: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity. However, accurate and reliable epidemic forecasting remains notoriously challenging and is an evolving field in which new scientific advances continue to support forecasting efforts. Computational models that underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models are promising developments that may improve seasonal epidemic forecasting. This study aims to compare the performance of a selection of AI models previously identified as well adapted to epidemic forecasting, including machine learning (XGBoost), deep learning models (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer), time-series foundation model (Chronos), and a hybrid model: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), against statistical models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Prophet) and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM) in seasonal epidemic forecasting across Canada. The study uses weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season as a test case. Each model generated short-term (up to 5 weeks ahead) forecasts independently for each province from October 11, 2025, to March 28, 2026. We evaluated performance using mean absolute error (MAE) for each province. Our results show that AI models, specifically GRU, Transformer, and Chronos models, achieve lower MAE than CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan). Meanwhile, CEM and ARIMA outperform all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia), respectively. Furthermore, data pooling strategies that leverage multi-province data for the target virus or multi-virus data within individual provinces greatly improve deep learning models, and Chronos performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia. In contrast, Prophet always has the highest MAE, and PINN is worse than CEMs. Overall, AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs. However, these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation. We therefore conclude that AI models are best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs, which remain crucial for interpretability and informing decision-making.

after.authors: Baldenweck, L.; Djisalov, M.; Pinamonti, D.; manzano, M.; Gadjanski, I.; Vidic, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: INRAE
after.abstract: An advanced LAMP assay targeting the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was developed and validated using clinical and foodborne S. aureus isolates. Reference strains, including both methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant S. aureus, were used to evaluate and optimize assay performance. With the newly designed ID16 LAMP primer set, the detection limit for mecA was 15 fg/L of total genomic DNA, equivalent to 5 copies/L, and the assay turnaround time was only 25 min. All mecA-positive isolates identified by conventional qPCR were successfully detected by the LAMP assay. Overall, the developed LAMP method provides a rapid, highly specific, and sensitive alternative for mecA detection.

after.authors: Sharma, A.; Nakiyingi, L.; Janeva, E. J.; Guevarra, K.; Nate, W.; Nabawanuka, E.; Shankman, R.; Dhamdhere, R.; Astorga, G.; Joloba, M. L.; Ellner, J.; Madabhushi, A.; Xie, Y. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Emory University
after.abstract: Rationale: Point of care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives: To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods: In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound only, and combined models and derived a 6 zone protocol from training set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results: Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80 to 0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) and 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) for the 12 zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test ([≥]90% sensitivity, [≥]60% specificity). Conclusion: Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed

after.authors: Romero Fragoso, I.; Sainz-Jimenez, A.; Reyes Cruz, T.; Chiquete, E.; Tamez-Torres, K.; Sifuentes-Osornio, J.; Fossion, R.; Estanol, B.; Aceves-Buendia, J. d. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Nacional de Ciencias Medicas y Nutricion Salvador Zubiran
after.abstract: Background: When aiming to quantify autonomic imbalance, conventional heart rate variability (HRV) analysis generally reduces each posture to a single spectral value derived from interbeat intervals (IBI) alone. This analysis based only in IBI obscures transient events during blood pressure changes. We propose two wavelet-derived indices that quantify cardiac vagal and vasomotor sympathetic oscillations separately and over time. Since autonomic imbalance is directly related to baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), we evaluated them against an estimate of baroreflex sensitivity in post-COVID-19 patients. Methods: In this study, 121 participants (32 healthy controls and 89 patients with persistent post-COVID-19 autonomic symptoms) underwent an active standing test with continuous finger blood pressure. The continuous wavelet transform with generalized Morse wavelets yielded time-varying high-frequency power of IBI and low-frequency power of systolic blood pressure (SBP). Two new indices were proposed: Index I combined the magnitude and variability of HF IBI power (aimed to quantify parasympathetic activity), and the index J combined LF SBP power with the rate of its transient elevations (bursts), which aims to quantify sympathetic vasomotor activity; J/I was their ratio. Indices were computed for supine and orthostatic periods and compared with conventional HRV and BRS measurements. Results: Index I correlated strongly with HF power of IBI and was lower in all patient subgroups than in controls, Index J had only a weak relation with LF power of IBI. On standing, J increased most in the subgroups with the worst baroreflex function. Orthostatic J/I was higher than in controls in all three subgroups, while LF/HF showed no differences. J/I was inversely correlated with BRS, most strongly when standing, and more strongly than LF/HF also. Adding J to I raised the cross-validated variance explained in orthostatic BRS substantially. In one example patient, a window during symptoms showed vasomotor oscillations that were hidden in the posture average. Conclusions: Wavelet-derived indices from routine beat-to-beat recordings separate cardiac vagal modulation from sympathetic vasomotor oscillations and their transients. J/I correlates with BRS impairment more closely than LF/HF, providing a potential alternative estimate of autonomic balance, and its time-resolved visual output allows analysis of clinically relevant windows within a posture. The new proposed variables allowed an evaluation of autonomic imbalance that could be applied to different pathologies. Keywords: continuous wavelet transform; heart rate variability; blood pressure variability; baroreflex sensitivity; Mayer waves; dysautonomia; long COVID; active standing test; autonomic imbalance.

after.authors: Melendez Loredo, A. V.; Salgado, R. C.; Calva, L. R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social
after.abstract:
BackgroundDescriptions of adolescent pregnancy can identify priorities for prenatal care and postpartum follow-up. This study characterized prenatal care and clinical outcomes documented in adolescent pregnancy records.

MethodsWe conducted a retrospective, descriptive, observational cross-sectional review of records covering 2020-2024 at a single family medicine outpatient service. All eligible records were included. Prenatal care and clinical characteristics were summarized using frequencies and percentages. Reporting was restricted to aggregate results to reduce the risk of participant identification.

ResultsThirty-nine records were analyzed. The first prenatal visit occurred in the second trimester in 53.85%. Overweight or obesity was recorded in 71.8%. Urinary tract infection occurred in 66.67% and gestational hypertension in 28.21%. No preterm births or obstetric hemorrhages were recorded. Vaginal delivery accounted for 51.28% and cesarean delivery for 48.72%. Postpartum contraceptive method was unspecified in 64.10% of records.

ConclusionsThis small, single-center study identified frequent urinary tract infections, a high recorded proportion of overweight or obesity, prenatal entry commonly after the first trimester, and incomplete postpartum contraceptive documentation. These findings identify local priorities for care and record quality; they do not establish causal relationships or population prevalence.

after.authors: Torii, S.; Hirano, R.; Angga, M. S.; Takeshita, K.; Yoshimi, K.; Kitajima, M.; Mashimo, T.; Oguma, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Tokyo
after.abstract: Test-strip-based CRISPR diagnostics could enable decentralized nucleic acid monitoring, but their application to environmental waters has been constrained by insufficient sensitivity and complex environmental matrices. Here, we developed a highly sensitive and specific assay combining reverse transcription-nested recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-nRPA) with Cas3-Operated Nucleic Acid detectioN (CONAN) for test-strip-based detection of Cryptosporidium 18S rRNA and pepper mild mottle virus (PMMoV). Introducing a second, nRPA step reduced the 50% limit of detection (LOD50) to 2.0 copies/reaction for Cryptosporidium and 1.5 copies/reaction for PMMoV. In 17 river water and six wastewater extracts, CONAN was positive for all nRPA products containing the Cryptosporidium sequence and negative for all products lacking the target. Cas12a-based DETECTR was negative for four Cryptosporidium-containing nRPA products, whereas LAMP and qPCR frequently cross-reacted with non-target environmental eukaryotic sequences. Consequently, nRPA-CONAN can overcome sensitivity and specificity constraints and offer a practical route toward instrument-light nucleic acid monitoring in environmental waters.

after.authors: Tran, B. M.; Nguyen, V. A.; Dang, Q. A.; Nguyen Ngoc, M. H.; Tran, H. N.; Tran, D. H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Hanoi University of Industry
after.abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and DNA methylation can provide complementary information for breast cancer prognosis, yet these measurements may be unavailable for new patients. In this paper, we propose HEAL-Surv, a teacher-student framework that uses both modalities during training to predict five-year net disease-specific survival (DSS) from clinical variables and molecular profiles at inference. An additive Cox teacher integrates all four modalities, using a hierarchical IMC graph encoder to capture local cell relationships and coarser tissue organisation. The student learns from observed outcomes and cross-fitted teacher survival curves, giving more weight to targets that agree across random initialisations. In five-fold cross-validation on 423 METABRIC patients, the full teacher achieved a mean five-year Uno's concordance of 0.723. Removing any modality reduced mean concordance and increased mean Brier-based errors. Relative to the matched student trained on observed outcomes alone, distillation increased mean five-year Uno's concordance from 0.658 to 0.704, with higher integrated and five-year Brier scores. In a separate external evaluation, an IMC-clinical variant trained on METABRIC achieved a five-year Uno's concordance of 0.660 on 265 Basel patients without refitting. These findings support multimodal supervision for improving risk discrimination with fewer inference inputs, while external validation of the student remains necessary.

after.authors: Walker, D.; Martins, P.; Khaledi, P.; Alexander, H.; Stirling, A.; Neller, M. A.; Kelly, J.; Biggs, V.; Reddiex, H.; Panikkar, A.; Beagley, L.; Flynn, S.; Raju, J.; Voogt, M.; Solomon, M.; Smith, C.; Khanna, R.

after.abstract: Purpose: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains refractory to immunotherapy due to its immunosuppressive microenvironment. Tumour-infiltrating cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells express elevated programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1), suggesting checkpoint-mediated dysfunction may limit T-cell therapy. We evaluated the safety and immunological activity of allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) combined with pembrolizumab. Patients and Methods: In this phase I 3+3 dose-escalation study, recurrent GBM patients received four weekly infusions of CYT-101 followed by pembrolizumab. The primary endpoint was safety. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival at 6 months (PFS-6), overall survival at 6 months (OS-6), and immune correlates of response. Results: CYT-101 T-cell therapy demonstrated polyfunctional activity, broad HLA restriction, potent cytolytic function, and diverse T-cell receptor repertoires. Nine patients received study treatment. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. Only six adverse events were considered treatment-related, and no treatment-related serious adverse events, graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, or neurotoxicity occurred. OS-6 and PFS-6 were 55% and 11%, respectively, with a median overall survival of 9.1 months. No objective clinical responses were seen. Of the nine treated participants, one had stable disease, five had progressive disease, and three were unevaluable by modified RANO criteria. Immune profiling revealed enhanced global CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell function following CYT-101 therapy, while donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected in six of nine participants, with significant T-cell repertoire remodelling. Conclusions: Allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy combined with pembrolizumab was safe in recurrent GBM, supporting further evaluation of this strategy to overcome immune dysfunction in GBM.

after.abstract: Microbiome modulation can augment responses to immunotherapy in advanced cancer. Early studies of anti-PD-1 therapies in combination with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) reported efficacy in immunotherapy-naive and -refractory settings. However, FMTs are variable in composition, difficult to scale, and risk the transfer of emerging pathogens. VE800 is a consortium of 11 strains of commensal bacteria derived from healthy donors and grown from clonal cell banks. VE800 increased anti-PD-1 efficacy in preclinical models of cancer. CONSORTiUM-IO was a first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study that evaluated safety and efficacy of VE800 with nivolumab in advanced PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma and PD-1-naive microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). VE800 plus nivolumab was well tolerated but offered no improvement over historic response rates. Exploratory analyses in patients with melanoma revealed that VE800 strain engraftment was associated with greater progression-free survival (PFS) and increased immune activation peripherally.

after.authors: Wang, W.; Olsman, R.; Grashof, D. G. B.; Scheffers, L.; Leenders, M.; Robbrecht, D. G. J.; Snaebjornsson, P.; Katsikis, P. D.; van de Wouw, Y. A. J.; van de Werken, H. J. G.

after.abstract: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. Conclusions: CUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

after.title: Preprint: Feasibility and Psychological Outcomes of a Clinical Meditation Intervention for Patients with Cancer: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
after.authors: Niida, A.; Koshiyama, T.; Baba, K.; Fujisawa, G.; Iwane, N.; Ohshita, D.; Shida, D.; Boku, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Laboratory of Molecular Medicine, Human Genome Center, The Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
after.abstract:
BackgroundPsychological care is an important component of cancer care, addressing psychological distress and supporting patients as they cope with illness. Meditation-based approaches, including mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), have been incorporated into supportive cancer care internationally. Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho), a meditation method developed in Japan, integrates traditional Buddhist meditation with a contemporary medical care perspective. However, its feasibility and psychological outcomes in patients with cancer have not been sufficiently studied.

ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Clinical Meditation intervention and to explore psychological outcomes and participants experiences among patients with cancer who were receiving or scheduled to receive pharmacotherapy at the time of recruitment.

MethodsThis single-arm pilot study used a convergent mixed-methods design to evaluate an 8-week program consisting of a 4-week structured phase (1 face-to-face session and 3 brief online group sessions, with prescribed home practice) and a 4-week self-directed phase (1 individual online session, with voluntary home practice). Feasibility was assessed descriptively using retention, attendance, practice frequency, and poststudy feedback. Anxiety, depression, insomnia, fatigue, spiritual well-being (SWB), and posttraumatic growth (PTG) were assessed at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. Changes were examined using Friedman tests and exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with adjustment for multiple comparisons. Free-text responses were analyzed thematically and integrated with questionnaire findings at the participant level.

ResultsEleven patients were enrolled; 9 (81.8%) completed the 4-week assessment and 8 (72.7%) completed the 8-week assessment. Median practice frequency declined from 5-6 days per week during the structured first month to 3-4 days per week during the self-directed second month (P=.031). Quantitative analyses included 9 participants, of whom 8 completed all 3 assessments; qualitative analyses included 8 participants. SWB and PTG showed significant overall changes (adjusted P=.02 and P=.04, respectively). SWB was higher than baseline at 4 weeks (adjusted P=.012), but the difference was not significant at 8 weeks. PTG was higher than baseline at both 4 and 8 weeks (both adjusted P=.047). No significant changes were observed in anxiety, depression, insomnia, or fatigue. Five themes were identified, encompassing experiences such as relaxation, greater distance from rumination, and meditation as a source of support. Participants accounts generally aligned with increases in SWB and PTG scores, although perceived benefits did not always correspond to changes in all questionnaire measures.

ConclusionsThis mixed-methods pilot study suggests that Clinical Meditation may be feasible and acceptable for patients with cancer, although sustaining meditation practice remains challenging. Exploratory increases in SWB and PTG warrant further investigation. Larger controlled studies, comparisons with established MBIs, and deeper qualitative research are needed to evaluate outcomes and clarify the distinctive features of Clinical Meditation.

after.authors: Chou, A. J.; DelRocco, N.; Krailo, M.; Buxton, A.; Hingorani, P.; Weigel, B. J.; Fox, E.; Lagmay, J. P.; Gorlick, R.; Roberts, R.; Dubois, S. G.; Reed, D.; Janeway, K. A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Dana-Farber / Boston Childrens Cancer and Blood Disorders Center
after.abstract: Objective: Osteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/Methods: This study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. Results: Ninety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. Conclusion: Despite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.

after.authors: Rhee, D.; Lewis, J.; De Francesco, T.; Nelson, K.; Ianchulev, T.; Sarkisian, S. R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: New York Eye and Ear of Mount Sinai
after.abstract:
PurposeTo characterize 12-month ocular safety of bio-interventional uveoscleral outflow enhancement in open-angle glaucoma (OAG).

DesignProspective, multicenter real-world evidence study (CREST; NCT05506423).

ParticipantsAdults with OAG treated by bio-interventional uveoscleral outflow enhancement with acellular scleral allograft spacers (AlloFlo, Iantrek, Inc.), standalone or with phacoemulsification, reaching 12 months of follow-up.

MethodsAdverse events were captured prospectively at each protocol-specified visit against pre-defined definitions; data were analyzed at the eye level.

Main Outcome MeasuresPre-specified ocular safety endpoints: adverse events, clinically significant hypotony, sustained intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation [≥] 10 mmHg beyond 30 days, allograft migration, corneal endothelial decompensation, secondary incisional glaucoma surgery, and endothelial cell density.

ResultsOf 395 eyes (mean age 72.8 years; 52% female), 267 were combined with phacoemulsification (Cohort 1) and 128 standalone (Cohort 2). Medicated IOP decreased from 19.1 to 14.5 mmHg (p < 0.001) and medications from 1.9 to 1.2, with 42% medication-free. Sustained IOP elevation occurred in 34 eyes (8.6%), BCVA loss [≥] 2 lines in 15 (3.8%), hyphema > 2 mm in 6 (1.5%) and hypotony in 1 (0.3%). Two allograft spacers entered the anterior chamber in one eye and were successfully repositioned intraoperatively. Serious events occurred in 12 eyes (3.0%). In the N=91 eyes with paired specular microscopy data, endothelial cell density changed -6.5% (-8.7%, -4.4%). There were no reports of endothelial decompensation, endophthalmitis, or sympathetic ophthalmia.

ConclusionsThrough 12 months no endothelial decompensation, endophthalmitis or sympathetic ophthalmia occurred, and most events were self-limiting or medically managed. Endothelial cell loss tracked concurrent cataract surgery rather than the allograft, though that subgroup is small. Follow-up remains shorter than the interval over which an earlier supraciliary microstent diverged from controls.

Trial RegistrationClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05506423.)

after.title: Preprint: Uveoscleral Outflow Enhancement as a Complementary Bio-intervention after Failed Prior Trabecular Outflow Treatment: 12-Month Outcomes of Allograft-reinforced Cyclodialysis in Open Angle Glaucoma
after.authors: Gazzard, G.; Jayaram, H.; Garg, R.; Ianchulev, T.; Stamper, R.; Tsai, J.; Singh, I. P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: New York Eye and Ear of Mount Sinai
after.abstract:
Abstract and KeywordsO_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSEyes with open-angle glaucoma uncontrolled after a trabecular outflow procedure have limited options before progressing to bleb-forming surgery. The uveoscleral pathway is distinct, relatively pressure-independent, and conjunctiva-sparing. We report 12-month outcomes of standalone allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis in eyes with IOP that remained uncontrolled after prior trabecular outflow intervention.

MethodsAnalysis of a multicentre registry (CREST; NCT05506423). Eligible eyes had at least one prior trabecular outflow procedure, no prior bleb-forming surgery, and underwent uveoscleral outflow bio-intervention with at least 12 months of follow-up. IOP reported as mean with 95% CI, medication as mean {+/-} SD.

ResultsForty-seven eyes were eligible; 91.5% completed 12 months. Consistent with moderate-to-advanced glaucoma, baseline IOP was 22.5 mmHg (20.1, 24.9) on 3.0 (1.3) IOP-lowering medications, with visual field mean deviation -11.7 dB (8.1). 95.7% were pseudophakic. In the per-protocol efficacy analysis, IOP fell 6.1 mmHg (3.7, 8.6), a 25.0% reduction (15.5%, 34.5%; p < 0.001), with no increase in medication. At 12 months, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of freedom from incisional reoperation was 78.2% (61.8%, 88.2%). There were no vision-threatening, clinically significant adverse events associated with the procedure such as persistent hypotony, maculopathy or other complications.

ConclusionsIn eyes with inadequately controlled IOP following prior trabecular intervention, standalone allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis was associated with clinically meaningful IOP reduction without an increase in medication burden or permanent vision loss.

after.authors: li, z.; ni, j.; wang, s.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital
after.abstract: Background: The purpose of this study was to assess the impact of intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) on postoperative drainage, laboratory parameters, and complications in patients undergoing immediate extended latissimus dorsi (ELD) flap breast reconstruction. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 82 patients who underwent immediate ELD flap breast reconstruction between January 2019 and May 2026. The TXA group (n = 42) received 1 g of intravenous TXA at the start of surgery after its routine adoption in July 2021; the control group (n = 40) underwent surgery before this date without TXA. Drainage, perioperative hemoglobin, hematocrit, and CRP levels, and postoperative complications were assessed using multivariable linear regression, with Cox regression as a complementary time-to-event analysis. Results: After adjustment for potential confounders, TXA use was associated with a shorter drain duration ({beta} = -1.85 days, 95% CI -3.09 to -0.61; p = 0.004) and lower total drainage volume ({beta} = -131.5 mL, 95% CI -247.2 to -15.8; p = 0.027). The adjusted Cox model also showed previous drain removal in the TXA group (HR = 2.59, 95% CI: 1.50-4.46; p < 0.001). Hematoma was found in 0 patients in the TXA group and 6 patients in the control group (p = 0.011); this result is to be regarded as descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Conclusion: This study provides some evidence that intravenous TXA reduces postoperative drainage and hematoma rates after immediate ELD flap breast reconstruction; however, prospective randomized studies are necessary to validate its safety profile and define its exact role.

S.; Jain, N.; Kaniewska, E.; Kleinjung, T.; Korn, J.; Ost, J.; Ralston Ruesch, L.; Rambour, S.; Shields, N.; Staudinger, S.; Tödtli, B.; Wolpert, S. M.; Yasoda-Mohan, A.; Husain, F. after.author_corresponding_institution: Karolinska Institutet
after.abstract: Tinnitus lacks an objective marker, limiting diagnosis and treatment evaluation. We tested whether gap-mediated inhibition of cortical sound-evoked responses provides one. In a prospective, multicentre case-control study at seven sites in the United States and Europe, adults with and without chronic tinnitus heard brief pulses preceded or not by a silent gap, embedded in broadband or narrowband carriers, during electroencephalography. The primary outcome was inhibition of the N100 response. Of 584 eligible participants, 455 yielded high-quality recordings with complete covariate data (232 cases, 223 controls; mean age 45.4 years, 52% women) that entered the adjusted analyses. Inhibition was strongest for broadband noise whereas narrowband carriers gave limited dynamic range. Participants with tinnitus showed reduced broadband gap-mediated inhibition ({beta} = -19.27%, d = -0.413, cluster-corrected p = 0.002), scaling with tinnitus severity (covariate-adjusted {surd}THI model: partial R2 = 0.049, p = 0.0015). In contrast, discrimination of individuals was limited (AUC 0.612, 95% CI 0.560-0.663). Cortical gap inhibition is a reproducible group-level effect rather than an individual diagnostic test.

after.authors: Xie, M. E.; Liang, H.; Wang, X.; Yedavalli, V.; Jackson, C.; Lim, M.; Huang, J.; Bettegowda, C.; Liu, P.; Xu, R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurosurgery, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD
after.abstract: Although the leading theory for the cause of trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is neurovascular compression, compression alone does not fully explain which nerves are painful. Recent work has demonstrated that pain in TN is associated with morphological changes of the trigeminal nerve, which may be a result of specific forms of compression or other disease processes. These changes have so far been quantified by hand-crafted geometric measurements, which can miss higher-order characteristics of the anatomy that are difficult to visualize. In this study, we use a cohort of 479 patients with TN who underwent microvascular decompression and had high-resolution pre-operative MRI scans to determine whether data-driven 3D shape features of the trigeminal nerve capture pain-associated morphology better than predefined metrics. We find that a predictive model using our shape features can distinguish nerves implicated in pain from those without pain in a held-out test cohort with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.719, compared with 0.626 for a model using existing hand-crafted measurements (p=0.005). Our study identifies candidate nerve morphology biomarkers of TN pain through data-driven shape analysis and demonstrates that these higher-order features relate better to symptoms of TN than conventional shape metrics.

after.title: Preprint: Exploring perceptions and attitudes toward pain in surgical trauma patients in a public hospital in Guatemala: a qualitative study
after.authors: Mahalingam, V.; Turner, R.; Zacarias, K.; Ramirez, S.; Simmons, C. G.; Gamboa, J. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Colorado School of Medicine
after.abstract:
Pain is nearly universal following traumatic injuries. However, pain perception, expression, and coping may be shaped by biological, psychological, social, and cultural factors that remain poorly characterized among underrepresented populations. This study explored experiences, attitudes, and expectations toward pain among hospitalized trauma patients at a public hospital in Guatemala.

We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with consenting adults admitted to the orthopedic trauma service at Hospital Nacional de Coatepeque in southwestern Guatemala from May to June 2025. Interviews explored pain experiences, coping strategies, interactions with healthcare providers, and expectations for pain management. Interviews were conducted in Spanish, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English by bilingual researchers, and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.

Five interrelated themes were identified: 1) lived experience and trajectory of pain; 2) coping, adaptation, and psychological endurance; 3) spirituality, meaning-making, and moral framing of suffering; 4) pain management and interactions with the healthcare system; and 5) social context, responsibilities, and life disruptions. Participants described severe early pain accompanied by physical, emotional, and functional distress that generally improved over time. Psychological coping, faith, and family responsibilities were central to resilience and recovery. Notably, patients often reported acceptable or improving numerical pain scores despite narratives describing substantial physical, emotional, and functional suffering, suggesting that standardized pain scales may not fully capture lived experiences.

Trauma patients in Guatemala described pain as a multidimensional experience shaped by physical, psychological, spiritual, and sociocultural factors. Despite severe pain, patients demonstrated resilience, often accepting pain as a temporary part of healing while prioritizing recovery and return to family responsibilities. The discordance between numerical pain scores and narratives of suffering underscores limitations of pain scores as standalone measures. These findings support culturally informed, patient-centered strategies that integrate pharmacologic treatment with attention to psychological, spiritual, and social dimensions of recovery.

after.authors: Chou, P. J.; Lin, Y. H.; Li, E. Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: National Chung Cheng University, Minhsiung, Chiayi 62130, Taiwan
after.abstract: Background: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems. Objective: Leveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics. Methods: The review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis. Results: Across 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes. Conclusion: This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human-AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

after.title: Preprint: Recording sampling rate as a negative-control exposure for detecting measurement-driven bias in heart-rate-variability-outcome associations: a quantitative bias analysis across ICU waveform databases
after.authors: Ye, H.; Zhang, Q.; Chen, S.; Li, P.; Wan, J.; Hao, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Critical Care Medicine, Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, 490 South Chuanhuan Road, Pu
after.abstract: Importance. Heart-rate variability (HRV) is studied extensively as a prognostic marker in critical illness, yet the electrocardiographic sampling rate at which HRV is computed systematically distorts the resulting values. Whether the associations between HRV and clinical outcomes reported in the literature are partly a consequence of this distortion has not been examined directly. Objective. To evaluate whether between-database differences in native ECG sampling rate can be used as a negative-control exposure to detect measurement-driven bias in HRV-outcome associations, and to quantify the sensitivity of a published association to an empirically measured distortion coefficient using quantitative bias analysis (QBA). Design. A methods investigation in three parts. Part I sets out the causal structure and states why a strict instrumental-variable (IV) design is inappropriate here. Part II derives a bias-correction factor under a multiplicative measurement-error model and propagates the empirical confidence interval of the distortion coefficient as a sensitivity band. Part III applies the procedure to an observed HRV-mortality association from a single ICU waveform database, and examines the separate bias arising from threshold-based categorisation. Setting and data sources. Two critical-care waveform databases with different native sampling rates (MIMIC-IV Waveform, approximately 250 Hz; MIMIC-III Waveform Matched p04, 125 Hz) and an independent 500-Hz reference cohort (PTB-XL) for mechanism validation. The outcome association was estimated in 1,445 ICU stays from MIMIC-III p04, of whom 141 died in hospital (9.8%). Exposures. Native ECG sampling rate as a negative-control exposure; SDNN, RMSSD and heart rate as the measured exposures whose associations with mortality are evaluated. Main outcomes and measures. In-hospital mortality. Distortion coefficients were obtained by end-to-end reprocessing of 7,293 original waveform segments with a fixed QRS detector. Corrected odds ratios were reported as QBA sensitivity bands rather than point-identified effects. Misclassification was quantified as the proportion of recordings below a 20 ms HRV threshold reclassified above it by coarse sampling. Results. End-to-end reprocessing gave an RMSSD distortion coefficient of 1.1575 (95% CI 1.0835-1.2492; 2,276 segments in 188 patients) for 250->62.5 Hz and 1.0588 (95% CI 1.0294-1.1033; 4,988 segments) for 125->62.5 Hz; high-frequency power was more affected than low-frequency power (1.2033 vs 1.0716). Under the multiplicative model, an observed crude RMSSD-mortality odds ratio of 1.802 corresponded to a corrected interval of 1.8335-1.915 across the coefficient's 95% CI. The correction was small relative to confounding: the same association fell to 1.116 after age adjustment. Coarse sampling reclassified 33.70% of low-HRV recordings in MIMIC-IV and 20.72% in MIMIC-III, a larger potential source of bias than the continuous-scale correction. The cross-database negative-control gradient was completed after linking both waveform cohorts to hospital outcomes: RMSSD inflation was reproducible (median x1.101 at 125->62.5 Hz in MIMIC-III and x1.270 at 250->62.5 Hz in MIMIC-IV), but the age-adjusted HRV-mortality risk ratio did not increase at lower rates (MIMIC-III 1.70->1.21; MIMIC-IV 1.31->1.29->1.20; all 95% CIs crossed 1). The falsification test was therefore negative in these cohorts, and we report it as such rather than as evidence that measurement bias is absent. Conclusions and Relevance. Sampling rate is a detectable and correctable source of bias in HRV-outcome research. Recording the sampling rate of each signal, stratifying effects by baseline variability, and reporting a QBA sensitivity band before dichotomising HRV would make published associations more interpretable. The object of inference here is the measurement-error method, not a new clinical biomarker; the proposed reporting steps require no additional data collection.

after.title: Preprint: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts
after.authors: Chen, A. F.; Yang, A.; Guth, D. R.; Berl, F. M.; Guth, S. C.; Yuan, W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: NYU Grossman School of Medicine
after.abstract: Objective To compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and Methods We evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. Results Claude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. Discussion SOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. Conclusion For biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.

after.title: Preprint: Changes in Medicaid GLP-1 Prescription Dispensing After 4 States Ended Weight-Management Coverage
after.authors: Lo, W.-L.; Conti, R. M.; Nguyen, T.; Gupta, S.; Wing, C.; Simon, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Indiana University
after.abstract: On January 1, 2026, California, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and South Carolina ended Medicaid coverage of GLP-1s indicated for weight management. In 2025 Q4 these four states accounted for 60.5% of Medicaid weight-management GLP-1 prescriptions nationally (661,478 of 1,094,191). We used State Drug Utilization Data from 2024 Q1 through 2026 Q1 to describe dispensing in the first quarter after withdrawal, classifying products by FDA-approved indication. In the withdrawing states, weight-management GLP-1 prescriptions were 1.06 per 100 enrollee-months in 2025 Q3, 1.08 in 2025 Q4, and 0.16 in 2026 Q1, a decline of 85%, while in six states that kept coverage the same figures were 0.90, 0.97, and 0.82. The difference-in-differences estimate was -0.67 (95% CI, -1.21 to -0.18). Gross reimbursement in the withdrawing states fell by $1,079 per 100 enrollee-months from 2025 Q3 to 2026 Q1. Dispensing of GLP-1s labeled for other indications did not rise: the estimate against 33 never-covering states was -0.03 (95% CI, -0.29 to 0.23), so increases larger than 0.23 per 100 enrollee-months, about one quarter of the weight-management decline, can be ruled out. Substitution toward diabetes-labeled products was at most limited in the first quarter after coverage ended.

after.title: Preprint: Whole-genome sequencing enables improved AML diagnostics and refines assessment of TP53 allelic state and complex karyotype
after.authors: Stanek, P.; Orsmark-Pietras, C.; Henningsson, R.; Rissler, M.; Landberg, N.; Agerstam, H.; Staffas, A.; Fogelstrand, L.; Palmqvist, L.; Barbany, G.; Knulst, M.; Juliusson, G.; Lazarevic, V.; Wirta, V.; Cavelier, L.; Rosenquist, R.; Lilljebjörn, H.; Fioretos, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Lund University
after.abstract: Accurate genetic characterization is central to modern acute myeloid leukemia (AML) diagnostics, yet current standard-of-care (SoC) testing relies on multiple complementary assays. We compared paired tumor-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with SoC diagnostics in a population-based cohort of 109 adult AML patients, assessing variant detection, disease classification according to ICC 2022 and WHO 2022, and risk stratification according to ELN 2022. WGS showed high concordance with SoC across variant classes. When considering all reported SoC variants together with high-confidence WGS variants as true positives, WGS showed equal to higher sensitivity than SoC for single-nucleotide variants and small insertions/deletions (97% vs 92%), structural variants (SVs; 100% vs 87%), and copy-number alterations (CNAs; 88.5% both). WGS identified clinically important lesions missed by SoC in 16 cases (15%), including FLT3-ITDs and KMT2A, NUP98 and MECOM rearrangements. Classification and risk assignments were 95-96% concordant, with WGS-driven reclassifications in 4-5% of cases, primarily through detection of cryptic SVs and myelodysplasia-related lesions. Integrated analysis of genomic alterations, including copy-neutral loss-of-heterozygosity, refined TP53 allelic state assessment and demonstrated increased genomic complexity in AML with biallelic TP53 alterations. We developed a supervised machine-learning model for complex karyotype (CK) probability, based on WGS-derived copy-number and SV burden, enabling automated identification of CK cases from WGS data. Collectively, these results support paired tumor-normal WGS as a single comprehensive assay well suited for AML diagnostics according to current classification and risk-stratification systems, while refining assessment of TP53 allelic state and karyotypic complexity.

after.authors: Asadikomeleh, S.; Neumann, T.; Krueger, W.; Ribback, S.; Schneidewind, L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Greifswald
after.abstract: Introduction: This is an immunohistochemical (IHC) pilot study of adult patients who underwent allogeneic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT) for hematological disease and had BKPyV reactivation (BKPyV viruria) as well as graft-versus-host-disease (GvHD) to investigate, if there is an association between these two diseases. Methods: The study was prospectively registered at the German Clinical Trials Register (https://drks.de/search/en/trial/DRKS00039127/details). The full protocol is available with this link. Results: Seven (58.3%) of the identified patients were treated in our prospective clinical trial regarding urological complications in alloSCT. All of them had BKPyV viruria during inpatient treatment for the transplantation and developed acute GvHD of the skin. Five (41.7%) of the patients were recruited in our prospective study of long-term survivors (more than five years) of alloSCT. All of them had BKPyV viruria as well as chronic GvHD of the skin at time of their examination. Acute myeloid leukemia was the most frequent underlying indication for alloSCT (n=7; 58.3%), followed by Non-Hodgkin-Lymphoma (NHL; n=2; 16,7%). Interestingly, IHC was negative for LTAg as well as VP1 in all patients. Therefore, it must also be stated that both virus proteins were negative in IHC for acute as well as chronic GvHD of the skin. Consequently, no further molecular investigations were realized. Conclusion: There is no evidence for an association between the viral proteins LTAg and VP1 of BKPyV and skin GvHD in immunohistochemistry. Due to the pilot character of our investigation, the results should be interpreted with great caution.

after.abstract: Respiratory viruses impose a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality globally, and models that forecast this burden are widely used to support public health decision-making. However, the public health utility of these forecasts can be limited by poor predictive accuracy. In this work, we show how capturing the effects of school holidays, public holidays and seasonal changes in transmission can improve respiratory virus forecasting performance. We construct a Bayesian renewal model where the effective reproduction number R(t) is composed of log-additive components including school and public holiday effects and an annually-periodic Gaussian process. The model also allows for the relative rate of reporting to vary with school and public holidays. We use this model to forecast respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza and SARS-CoV-2 case incidence across a 28-day horizon over five jurisdictions in Australia. Applied to the 2025 winter season, our forecasts outperform a random-walk baseline forecast across all settings. We find that the inclusion of holiday and seasonal transmission effects improved forecasting performance across the three pathogens. We show that the school holidays are associated with population-wide reductions in R(t) on the order of 5-15% but are generally not associated with changes in reporting. Collectively, our results provide support for the inclusion of holiday and seasonal effects in future respiratory virus forecasting models.

after.abstract: Background Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are standard therapy for primary aldosteronism (PA). Serum potassium is measured in nearly every treated patient, but the long-term prognostic value of potassium attained early after initiation is undefined. Methods In the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with PA newly initiating spironolactone or eplerenone in 2000-2025, without prior adrenalectomy (n=4,169; 180-day landmark design). Achieved potassium (last value on days 14-180) was categorised as <4.0, 4.0-<4.5, 4.5-<5.0 and [≥]5.0 mmol/L, and its change from baseline in tertiles, using cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke or death; incident heart failure was co-primary. Findings Over a median 3.0 years, 623 composite events occurred. Estimated risk was lowest at 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L (adjusted hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.52-0.83, versus <4.0 mmol/L), lower than the 4.0-<4.5 mmol/L band, and not different from [≥]5.0 mmol/L. A larger rise in potassium was associated with lower risk. A similar pattern was seen for incident heart failure (0.54, 0.36-0.80; 248 events). Potassium below the 3.6 mmol/L consensus threshold for hypokalaemia carried no significantly higher risk (1.22, 0.96-1.56). The change in potassium correlated weakly with the change in renin (rho = 0.15). Interpretation In MRA-treated PA, cardiovascular and heart-failure risk was lowest at an early achieved potassium of 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L, well above the 3.6 mmol/L accepted by consensus criteria as correction of hypokalaemia; correction alone may therefore be an insufficient treatment target. Whether titrating therapy towards this band improves outcomes requires prospective evaluation.

after.abstract: Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB) represents a global public health threat, with a rising prevalence, particularly among vulnerable populations. This cross-sectional study analyzed MDR-TB notifications in Brazil from 2001 to 2021, using data from DATASUS, and stratified by periods and risk groups (HIV-positive individuals, smokers, drug users, healthcare workers, incarcerated individuals, and people experiencing homelessness). Descriptive analyses and parametric statistical tests (ANOVA and Tukey, p less than 0.05) were applied. A significant increase in cases was observed across all groups, especially between 2017 and 2021, with growth ranging from 294% to 574% depending on the population. Factors such as treatment abandonment, coinfection, social vulnerability, and occupational exposure were key determinants for MDR-TB dissemination. The findings indicate that current public health policies are insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for targeted prevention strategies, therapeutic follow-up, and control measures for high-risk populations.

after.title: Preprint: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
after.authors: Baby, J. G.; Jaeckle, F.; Williams, J.; Shepherd, K.; Urwin, H.; Soilleux, E. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Cambridge
after.abstract: Objective: Biopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and normal). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology. Methods and Analysis: We conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients and carers questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources. Results: Most patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term machine learning being preferred to artificial intelligence. Agreement (agree or strongly agree combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p<0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI assistant model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight. Conclusion: Patients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry; Institute for Genomic Medicine, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
after.abstract: Wisdom is a personality trait composed of self-reflection, pro-social behaviors, emotional regulation, acceptance of divergent perspectives, decisiveness, social advising, and spirituality. Greater levels of wisdom are linked to better overall health, well-being, happiness, life satisfaction, and resilience. However, the underlying genetic architecture of wisdom remains unexplored. We assessed wisdom using responses to the SD-WISE-7 in 153,384 23andMe research-consented participants and conducted a multi-ancestry GWAS. We identified one genome-wide significant locus (rs2325631, p=1.41E-08) near MANEA on chromosome 6. Wisdom was heritable (h2SNP=0.03{+/-}4.50E-03) and genetically correlated with numerous traits, including greater subjective well-being, openness, and risk tolerance, and lower neuroticism and loneliness. Crucially, wisdom was genetically distinct from intelligence and the cognitive component of educational attainment. Wisdom polygenic scores were associated with psychosocial outcomes, but not cognitive performance in All of Us. This study advances our understanding of wisdom as a heritable trait that could guide interventions to improve human health.

after.abstract: Background: Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infection and a cause of adverse reproductive outcomes. Epidemiologic studies describe bacterial vaginosis (BV) as a major risk factor for CT infection. Emerging data suggest that BV-associated bacteria and their metabolites contribute to CT susceptibility. Here, we measured the role of specific bacteria in incident CT and evaluated a hypothesized causal role between the vaginal microbiota, its metabolites, and CT risk. Methods: We conducted a nested case-control study of Kenyan women who engage in transactional sex from the Mombasa Cohort who acquired CT versus those who did not, and compared their vaginal microbiome and metabolome at the visit preceding CT acquisition. We determined CT infection and total bacterial load using qPCRs. 16S rRNA sequencing was used to characterize the genital microbiome, and BV status was determined using Nugent-Hillier and Amsel scoring criteria. Metabolites were measured using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from a subset of women. Findings: Women with BV, high vaginal microbial diversity, and community state types III and IV were significantly more likely to have CT at their next visit. CT infection itself did not alter vaginal microbial diversity. More specifically, both concentrations and relative abundances of Lactobacillus crispatus and several BV-associated bacteria (Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella/Prevotella timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum) were predictive of CT outcomes. Vaginal metabolites differed between cases and controls pre-CT, including Tyramine, reduced and oxidized Glutathione, and sucrose. In a mediation analysis, the vaginal metabolome significantly mediated the relationship between the microbiome and CT infection. Interpretation: We show for the first time that the association between BV and CT risk is mediated by differences in the metabolome. Identification of the mechanisms underlying increased CT risk with BV can inform interventions to reduce infections in high-risk women. Funding: US NIH (R01AI13214401-A1)
