after.authors: Kalsoom, Z.; Khan, M. M.; Rashid, S. R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Microbiology, University of Agriculture Faisalabad, Faisalabad, Pakistan
after.abstract: Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria whose antibiotic susceptibility varies between clinical settings. We studied urinary isolates from 95 patients with suspected infection at Lahore General Hospital, Pakistan, between July and December 2023. Urine culture showed significant bacterial growth in 63 specimens (66.3%). Escherichia coli accounted for 30 isolates, followed by 18 Klebsiella isolates, comprising 16 Klebsiella pneumoniae and two Klebsiella oxytoca. Klebsiella was recovered from 12 female and six male patients, and the largest number of Klebsiella isolates occurred in patients aged 21-30 years. The aggregate susceptibility results, recorded for 18 isolates per antibiotic, showed the highest susceptibility to imipenem and meropenem (17/18 each), followed by nitrofurantoin (16/18). Resistance to several cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides was frequent. These findings describe the bacterial distribution and reported susceptibility patterns in a small hospital sample. Larger studies with verified species-specific susceptibility data are needed before these findings can guide local treatment policy.

after.abstract: Background The traditional business model for sustaining United States (U.S.) community pharmacies has relied on income generated by product sales. A fee-for-service model could help alleviate insufficient profit by monetizing conventionally free pharmacy services if patients are willing to pay out-of-pocket. Objectives This study evaluated public acceptability of out-of-pocket payment for community pharmacist-provided services, variation in payment acceptability across services, and assessed whether payment acceptability differed by respondent characteristics and trust constructs. Methods This study represents a cross-sectional online survey of U.S. adults conducted during spring 2026 using a non-probability sampling approach. Primary outcomes were binary stated payment-acceptability judgments for a variety of pharmacist and health services. The survey used a between-subjects randomized payment-framing design, where participants were assigned to either a stated-price condition or an any-payment condition. Secondary outcomes included trust designations and participant demographic characteristics. Results A total of 1069 respondents completed the survey. A $20 fee was viewed more favorably than a general "any amount of money" fee. after.abstract: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, yet no therapy targets its underlying autoimmune mechanisms. We combined transcriptomic analyses of rheumatic mitral valves tissues with a translational approach. Using a panel of 750 mRNAs, we found a marked upregulation of B-cell-related pathways, including CD20-associated and multiple immunoglobulin genes, supporting a pathogenic role of B cells in RHD. We therefore evaluated an anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody (Rituximab), in a feasibility study in children with RHD, in Dakar, Senegal. Treatment was well tolerated, and in the following RCT first year preliminary safety analysis asked by the ethical committee, children who received rituximab showed a decrease in anti-streptolysin O titers and clinical improvement compared to controls. This proof-of-concept reveals B cells as a therapeutic target and suggests that an anti-CD20 agent may represent a potential disease-modifying therapy for RHD.

after.title: Preprint: Cardiorespiratory Limits Exist in HFpEF Independent of Age and BMI
after.authors: LaGalbo, S.; Gowda, M.; Hess, T.; Tipnis, P.; Raza, F.; Saleh, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Wisconsin Hospitals and Clinics
after.abstract: Background: Heart-failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome marked by exercise intolerance associated with impairments in cardiac and respiratory performance. HFpEF is associated with age and weight; however, it remains unclear whether cardiorespiratory limitations exist independent of these comorbidities. Hypothesis: Independent of age and BMI, there are cardiorespiratory limitations inherent to the HFpEF syndrome that have yet to be fully elicited. Methods: A patient cohort with a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF (HFpEF; N = 38) and counterparts without identifiable cardiopulmonary disease (control; N = 21) underwent phenotyping with echocardiography and cardiopulmonary exercise testing with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. Results: Study cohorts were similar in age, BMI and height (p=NS for all metrics). Body-surface area (BSA) (2.1 m2 v 1.9 m2, p < 0.05), atrial fibrillation prevalence (50 v 14%, p < 0.05), and average E/e (11.5 v 9.5, p < 0.05) were elevated within the HFpEF cohort. Peak VO2 (14.1 v 19.1 mL/Kg/min, p < 0.001) was also diminished among those with HFpEF. Resting (17.1 v 11.4mmHg, p < 0.001) and exercise wedge pressures (29.3 v 16.7mmHg, p < 0.001) were elevated whereas stroke volume (93.3 v 110.4 mL, p < 0.05) and cardiac output (Direct Fick; 8.0 v 9.8, p < 0.05) during exercise were diminished in HFpEF patients. FVC, FVC%, FEV1 and FEV1% were also significantly diminished in the HFpEF cohort. Conclusions: Cardiorespiratory limitations exist as a feature of the HFpEF syndrome, independent of age and BMI. BSA remained associated with HFpEF in keeping with adiposity as a feature of pathophysiology.

after.title: Preprint: Charted times of bedside pain assessments are slot labels: prevalence across hospitals, consequences for estimating analgesic onset, and when hourly charting is an adequate approximation
after.authors: Lee, Y.; Moe, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: RIT
after.abstract: Objective. Temporal and causal analyses of electronic health records (EHRs) treat the charted time of an observation as the time it was made. We quantified how often bedside pain and sedation assessments are charted to a time slot, how this affects estimates of analgesic onset, and when hourly charting is an adequate approximation. Methods. We used intensive care unit (ICU) data from one academic center (MIMIC-IV) and 78 hospitals (eICU-CRD). Slot labeling was identified from charted minutes and from the delay between charted and entry times. In MIMIC-IV, opioid administration times served as anchors, and faster onset of intravenous (IV) than oral opioids as a pharmacologic benchmark. We compared onset estimated from charted times with onset from exactly timed records, bounded true assessment times under alternative charting mechanisms, and used simulation to relate bias to the ratio of slot width to response time constant ({Delta}/k). Results. In MIMIC-IV, 68% of pain and 76% of sedation scores were charted on the hour and entered a median of 41-44 minutes later. Of the first reassessments after a dose, 32-34% of on-hour records carried a time before the dose, against 12-14% of off-hour records. Across eICU hospitals, the on-hour share ranged from 15% to 92% (10th-90th percentile). By charted time, oral opioids appeared nearly as fast as IV (pain change at 15-30 minutes, -1.76 vs -2.11 points); exactly timed records showed -0.80 vs -2.00. Slower oral onset held under every charting mechanism compatible with the data, but its magnitude was not identified (ratio of time constants 1.2-11.6). In simulation, analysis by charted time was adequate up to {Delta}/k {approx} 2 when rounding was to the nearest slot, but only up to {Delta}/k {approx} 0.1 when rounding had a direction. Conclusion. Charted times of bedside assessments are often slot labels, and charting practice is hospital-specific. For ICU analgesic onset, neither condition for an adequate approximation can be assumed, and EHR data alone cannot recover the size of the effect.

after.title: Preprint: Accurate Prediction of Hepatic Disease Severity in MASLD Using a Learned Phenotype
after.authors: Strobl, E. V.; Miedel, M.; Taylor, D. L.; Behari, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pittsburgh
after.abstract: Background & Aims: Most prognostic models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) target prespecified hepatic endpoints, potentially limiting attainable accuracy. We developed and externally validated a model that learns the future hepatic phenotype most reliably predictable from baseline clinical characteristics. Methods: We analyzed 332 HALO-MASLD participants (456 follow-up observations). Sparse Canonical Outcome REgression (SCORE) learned a weighted phenotype from eight hepatic measures, coupled with broken adaptive ridge regression using 99 baseline predictor columns. Participant-level nested five-fold cross-validation compared prediction of the learned phenotype with future liver stiffness measurement (LSM), controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), and FIB-4 benchmarks. Models were externally validated without refitting in the independent NIDDK NAFLD Adult Database 2 cohort (520 participants, 732 follow-up observations). Biological validity and bootstrap stability were also assessed. Results: The learned phenotype emphasized lower platelet count and higher bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and LSM. In HALO, predictive correlation was r=0.860 (95% CI [0.824, 0.896]) and predictive R^2=0.671, versus r=0.763 for LSM and r=0.469 for CAP predicted from all baseline variables. All six prespecified comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (p_Holm < 0.05). The phenotype correlated with MRE stiffness (rho = 0.694) and biopsy fibrosis stage (rho = 0.567), and was higher with imaging evidence of portal hypertension (p < 0.001). Bootstrap relearning yielded mean phenotype correlation 0.947. In NIDDK, predictive correlation was r = 0.836 (95% CI [0.805, 0.863]; predictive R^2 = 0.680), and associations with fibrosis and portal hypertension replicated. Conclusions: Learning the prediction target produced a sparse, clinically interpretable hepatic phenotype more accurately predicted than conventional longitudinal MASLD endpoints in both cohorts. The resulting LIFT-MASLD model is available at https://liftmasld.github.io.

after.authors: Saraei, M.; Zand, M.; Rahmani, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Arizona
after.abstract: Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) enables simultaneous biomarker profiling, yet unmixing co-localized targets with identical spectra, such as dual-DAB marking of Tau and Amyloid-beta in Alzheimer's pathology, remains mathematically ill-posed. We propose MorphoStain, an unsupervised, physics-guided framework for morphological stain decomposition with epistemic uncertainty quantification. MorphoStain models stain separation via a conditional Latent Diffusion Teacher operating on a Beer-Lambert optical-density manifold, guided by pathology foundation models. To enable real-time clinical throughput, the teacher is distilled into a FastStudentU-Net (0.12M parameters, > 1,400x compression), while a Symmetric Morphological Routing Module dynamically disentangles identical chromogen overlap. Evaluated on 9,908 held-out patches from the SEA-AD cohort, MorphoStain achieves 40.56 dB PSNR and 0.9961 SSIM at 140.1 FPS, showing statistically significant gains over InverseAE (Cohen's d = 3.52) and NMF (Cohen's d = 7.02), with p < 0.001 for both comparisons.

after.authors: De Los Reyes, F. V. A.; Hayashi, S.; Kato, M.; Tanboon, J.; Noguchi, S.; Nishino, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neuromuscular Research, National Institute of Neuroscience, National Center of Neurology and Psychiatry; Kodaira, Tokyo, Japan
after.abstract: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is a progressive autoimmune myositis refractory to conventional immunosuppression, yet mechanisms sustaining chronic inflammation remain unresolved. Integrating comparative single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and orthogonal validation across autoimmune myositis, we identified ZNF683+IL7R+ cytotoxic tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells with natural killer cell-like features enriched in IBM. Trajectory analysis positioned an early-disease ZBTB16+ cytotoxic T cell state upstream of ZNF683+IL7R+TRM. ZNF683 overexpression induced memory and natural killer cell-like transcriptional programs while attenuating glucocorticoid-response signatures, linking this program to treatment refractoriness. Ligand-receptor modeling nominated candidate targetable circuits involving IL-15-IL15RA, XCL1-XCR1, and HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4. Spatial transcriptomics localized ZNF683+TRM to stress-associated IBM niches. These findings define a disease-specific TRM-centered circuit linked to treatment refractoriness and candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities in IBM.

after.authors: Delassus, O.; Sadoine, J.; Paternoster, G.; Chollet, L.; Ndambidi Yungi, B.; Beaufort, Q.; Taverne, M.; Boddaert, N.; Mangin, J.-F.; Khonsari, R. H.; Germanaud, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, Joliot Institute, NeuroSpin, UNIACT
after.abstract: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non FGFR related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1 weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype dependent brain anomalies in FGFR related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

after.title: Preprint: Sex and Gender Reporting and Female Participation Relative to Disease Burden in ClinicalTrials.gov
after.authors: Green, M. D.; Aziz, M.; Sullenger, R. D.; Yoo, B. J.; O'Brien, E. C.; Navar, A. M.; Duroseau, B.; Thorpe, R. J.; Brantner, C. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
after.abstract: Importance: Assessing representation by sex assigned at birth and gender identity requires reporting of both in trials. If disclosure of full gender and sex participation from clinicaltrials.gov is limited, it poses challenges in characterization and understanding of those participant experiences. Objective: To determine how often ClinicalTrials.gov trials published trials report sex and gender, which characteristics are associated with reporting, and how participants' female share compares with that of the general public. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered to ClinicalTrials.gov, with or without US sites, with primary completion on or after September 27, 2008, and results first posted from January 1, 2009, through April 30, 2026. Exposures: Funder type, phase, US sites, enrollment, primary completion year, number of countries, and therapeutic area. Main Outcomes and Measures: Reporting of sex and gender, and the female participation-to-prevalence ratio (PPR; trial female share divided by the number of people with the condition). Results: Among 58,007 trials (median enrollment, 72 [IQR, 31 to 206]; 42,644 [74%] with US sites), 553 (0.95%) reported gender and 57,683 (99.44%) reported sex. Gender reporting was more common with National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding (odds ratio [OR], 9.05; 95% CI, 6.65 to 12.6), US sites (OR, 4.21; 95% CI, 2.96 to 6.22), and larger enrollment. Across 10 conditions (15,552 mixed-sex trials), median PPR ranged from 0.68 (95% CI, 0.64 to 0.71) for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to 1.05 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.09) for obesity and had a relatively lower female share in 8. Among the 10 conditions most prevalent in our cohort, 6,917 of 16,097 trial condition combinations (43.0%) reached a PPR of at least 0.90; odds of reaching it were higher for NIH-funded (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11 to 1.34) and lower for government-funded trials (OR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.33) as compared to industry-funded trials. Conclusions and Relevance: In ClinicalTrials.gov, sex reporting is nearly universal, whereas gender reporting is concentrated among NIH-funded, US-based, and larger trials. Female trial enrollment fell below the female share of people with the condition for most conditions, emphasizing the benefit of condition-specific benchmarks in clinical trials.

after.title: Preprint: Cell-free telomeric DNA and integrity indices in axial spondyloarthritis: associations with somatic and mental burden: a case-control study.
after.authors: Husakova, M.; Banerjee, B.; Skubica, P.; Pavelka, K.; Kucharikova, K.; Kotrs, J.; Senolt, L.; Olejarova, M.; Mohr, P.; Dankova, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: First Faculty of Medicine, Charles University and Rheumatology Institute, Na Slupi 4, Prague, Czech Republic
after.abstract: Objectives: Depression and anxiety in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) are associated with higher disease activity. This study examined whether circulating cell-free nuclear DNA (cf-nDNA), mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA), relative telomere length (T/S ratio), and DNA integrity index (DII) are associated with mental burden and disease characteristics in axSpA. Methods: Plasma cf-nDNA, cf-mtDNA, T/S ratio, and ALU-247/ALU-115 ratio (DII) were analysed in 79 patients with axSpA and 88 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs). Mental burden was assessed using the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview (M.I.N.I.), Beck Depression Inventory-II, and Beck Anxiety Inventory. Clinical measures included the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score with C-reactive protein (ASDAS-CRP), and radiographic disease pattern. Results: Sex differences were observed in disease phenotype and hip involvement. Affective or anxiety disorders were more frequent in axSpA vs. HC (26.6% vs. 2.3%, p<0.001); depressive symptoms were also more frequent (20.2% vs. 2.27%, p<0.001) and higher in active vs. inactive disease (30.0% vs. 3.45%, p<0.001). Compared with HCs, patients had higher cf-mtDNA and lower DII (both p<0.01), with a trend towards lower T/S ratio. Females had higher T/S ratio and DII than males, and higher cf-mtDNA overall. Lower T/S ratio was associated with affective disorders, while only CRP independently predicted depressive symptom severity. Conclusions: Altered cfDNA profiles, particularly increased cf-mtDNA and reduced DII, are associated with axSpA, disease activity and mental burden, supporting their potential as biomarkers of disease-related processes.

after.title: Preprint: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
after.authors: Quagraine, I.; Guha, A.; Kilbane, C.; Ghasia, F. F.; Shaikh, A. G.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Case Western Reserve University
after.abstract: Objective: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results: Combined saccade vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7 to 49.3%; p=0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

after.title: Preprint: Plasma Proteomic Identifies GDF15 as a Candidate Lithium Treatment Response Biomarker in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Secondary Analysis of the LATTICE Randomized Clinical Trial
after.authors: Sehrawat, A.; Shi, R.; Farinas, M. F.; Emanuel, J. E.; Zeng, X.; Lopresti, B. J.; Royse, S. K.; Weinstein, A. M.; Butters, M. A.; Lee, L.; Gildengers, A. G.; Karikari, T. K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pittsburgh
after.abstract: Lithium (Li) demonstrates neuroprotective effects relevant to Alzheimer disease (AD). However, its molecular mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study analyzed plasma proteomic profiles from the Li as a Treatment to Prevent Impairment of Cognition in Elders (LATTICE) randomized clinical trial to identify markers associated with amyloid beta pathology, disease progression, and response to Li treatment. In the LATTICE trial, 80 older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) were randomly assigned to receive either low-dose Li carbonate or placebo for two years. Longitudinal plasma samples were analyzed using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120 proteomic panel. Baseline protein levels were compared according to randomized treatment assignment, amyloid beta PET status, and MCI subtype. Analyses included longitudinal changes in protein levels associated with treatment and time, associations between baseline protein levels and subsequent cognitive, functional, and neuroimaging trajectories, and the influence of baseline protein levels on Li treatment effects. Among the 80 participants, 62 had amnestic MCI and 21 were positive on amyloid beta PET. Baseline proteomic differences were more strongly associated with amyloid beta PET status than with randomized treatment assignment. Plasma p-tau217 concentrations were elevated in individuals who were positive on amyloid beta PET and remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Over time, CALB2 and TREM2 exhibited nominal treatment-by-time interactions in the full cohort, while in the amnestic MCI subgroup, CALB2, TREM2, and amyloid beta 40 demonstrated nominal effects. None persisted after multiple-testing correction. GDF15 showed the most consistent associations with CDR Sum of Boxes trajectories and treatment-effect modification that remained significant after false discovery rate correction in the amnestic MCI subgroup, whereas p-tau217 was most consistently associated with hippocampal volume trajectories. Other protein-outcome associations were exploratory. Plasma proteomics identified distinct molecular patterns associated with amyloid beta pathology and the MCI phenotype, along with exploratory evidence of Li-associated protein changes. Plasma GDF15 and p-tau217 emerged as potential markers of clinical progression and treatment-response heterogeneity, warranting validation in larger, adequately powered trials.

after.title: Preprint: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
after.authors: Zhou, D. J.; Jaskir, M.; Hutchinson, R.; Eisenberg, E. S.; Gal, J.; Imtiaz, T. J.; Goldblum, Z.; Vadali, C.; Lucas, A.; Josyula, M.; Gugger, J. J.; Conrad, E. C.; Das, S.; Stein, J. M.; Davis, K. A.; Sinha, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pennsylvania
after.abstract: Background and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

after.title: Preprint: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
after.authors: Vazquez, J.; Soldan, A.; Albert, M.; Lu, H.; Pantelyat, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
after.abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

after.title: Preprint: Hidden Dependencies in Endometriosis Microarray Classifiers: Sample Reuse, Outcome-Informed Batch Correction, and Diagnostic Reassessment
after.authors: Krikun, E.; Alkhateeb, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Lakehead University
after.abstract: Distinct Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) accessions do not necessarily represent independent transcriptomic samples. We investigated exact array reuse, access to test diagnoses during batch correction, and cohort and acquisition-date confounding in endometriosis classifiers. We compared decompressed CEL files using SHA-256, reconstructed a matrisome elastic-net workflow, changed test labels supplied to ComBat, and conducted 3,582 constrained training-label refits. We also evaluated the effect of removing matching training copies in a five-gene Huang-inspired random forest and performed a 324-probe nested internal benchmark within GSE51981. Of 37 test CEL files, 26 (70.3%) were identical to training arrays; all had been scanned in 2004-2005. Changing a test diagnosis supplied to ComBat moved the fixed classifier score toward the supplied label in all 37 interventions. In a deduplicated, batch-constrained comparison, median nominal balanced accuracy was 0.881 when ComBat received true test outcomes and 0.549 without them; the outcome-informed arm performed better in 1,193 of 1,194 matched refit comparisons. In the separate Huang-inspired reconstruction, removing each target's matching training copy lowered pooled AUC from 1.000 to 0.323 (conditional 95% interval 0.105-0.571). Exploratory nested AUC was 0.733 for endometriosis versus other gynecological conditions, and date-held-out AUC in 2009 was 0.698. For endometriosis versus healthy controls, a date-only out-of-fold model achieved AUC 0.935, compared with 0.893 for the molecular model. Together, these findings show how exact array reuse, outcome-informed preprocessing, and acquisition-date structure can compromise the interpretation of nominally independent validation. after.authors: Tapiavala, V. N.; Bather, J.; Ricci-De Lucca, E.; Murnane, E. L.; Goodman, M. S.; Fortuna, K. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Patient Innovation Lab, Department of Community and Family Medicine, Geisel School of Medicine, Lebanon, NH, USA.
after.abstract: Importance: Meaningful patient and community involvement is increasingly emphasized in health research. Still, little is known about how such research involvement relates to the quality of patient and community partnerships. Objective: To examine the associations of patient and community involvement in research with partnership outcomes. The associations of patient involvement in specific research phases (e.g., grant writing, recruitment, and data collection) with these metrics were examined as a secondary objective. Design: This cross-sectional observational study used baseline data from a national cohort study across the United States collected from September to December 2024. Setting: This national study was conducted online with recruitment occurring over multiple channels. Participants: Participants included patient and community research partners aged 18 years and older and were recruited in a convenience sample. Exposures: The extent to which participants have contributed to prior research studies were calculated by adding binary indicators representing their involvement in phases of the research process. These indicators were examined individually as secondary exposures. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Primary outcomes included partnership quality and research engagement, with trust in medical researchers and partnership recommendation as secondary and tertiary outcomes. Multivariable linear and modified Poisson regressions were utilized to estimate regression coefficients and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs). Results: Among 330 participants (mean age = 36.5 years, SD = 9.7), 56.1% were male, and 37.3% and 31.8% were White or Black, respectively. Involvement in patient-centered outcomes research was associated with partnership quality ({beta}, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.30-1.42, P=0.003), research engagement ({beta}, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.01-0.06, P=0.006), trust in medical researchers ({beta}, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.31-1.07, P<0.001), and greater willingness to recommend becoming a research partner (aPR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.05-1.14, P<0.001). Conclusions and Relevance: Patient-centered outcomes research may provide patient and community research partners with a sense of shared ownership, improving partnership quality. While the causal links require further investigation, these associations may be driven by inclusion in recruitment, grant writing, data collection, and shared governance.

after.title: Preprint: Rising Tuberculosis Presentations in Ontario, Canada Are Not Explained by Community SARS-CoV-2 Activity: A Population-Based Time-Series Study
after.authors: Wilson, N. J.; Tuite, A.; Lee, C. E.; Berkowitz, R. J.; Wiebe, B.; Hall, J.; Boushy, D.; Fisman, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Toronto
after.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis (TB) notifications have increased in several high-income countries since 2020. Proposed explanations include pandemic related disruption of treatment for latent tuberculosis, changes in population composition, and immune dysfunction following SARS CoV 2 infection. We assessed whether TB presentations increased during the pandemic era and then tested whether community SARS CoV 2 activity was followed by increased mycobacterial disease. Methods: We conducted a population-based ecological time-series study of first TB- and nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM)-coded hospital, emergency-department and ambulatory clinic presentations in the Greater Toronto/Hamilton Area Plus (GTHA+), Ontario (2024 population approximately 11.2 million), from April 2011 through March 2024. NTM served as a comparator because it shares diagnostic pathways with TB but differs epidemiologically. Negative binomial projection and full-series models estimated pandemic-era changes under three alternative trend assumptions. Distributed lag non linear models estimated cumulative rate ratios for standardized community viral activity over 0 to 12 weeks; sensitivity analyses extended the maximum lag to 26 and 52 weeks. Influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) were prespecified comparators; data for five additional viral exposures were obtained after the primary analysis was completed and analysed as exploratory comparisons. Results: We identified 3,985 first TB-coded and 5,214 first NTM-coded acute-care presentations. Across six models, estimated pandemic-era TB increases ranged from 3% to 22%. No model suggested an increased in NTM. SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with TB (cumulative rate ratio per 1-SD increase over 0 to 12 weeks 0.909, 95% CI 0.822 to 1.006) or NTM (0.953, 0.868 to 1.047). No positive associations were identified in subgroup analyses or with maximum lags of 26 or 52 weeks. Influenza was not associated with either outcome. RSV was associated with TB and NTM; only the RSV/NTM association met the Bonferroni threshold among the prespecified comparisons, and no exploratory associations met the experiment wide threshold. Conclusions: We identified a modest pandemic era increase in TB-coded acute-care presentations in Ontario, Canada, although its estimated size depended on assumptions about underlying trends. NTM-coded presentations did not increase. Community SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with subsequent TB or NTM presentations at lags of up to one year and did not provide a temporal explanation for the population-level TB increase. Individual-level effects cannot be excluded.

after.authors: Gonzalez-Diaz, A.; Broner, S.; Calvo-Silveria, S.; Grau, I.; Quesada, M. D.; Belles, A.; del Corral, E.; Pico-Plana, E.; Clapes, E.; Vinado, B.; Berbel, D.; Llopis, M. A.; Dominguez, M. A.; Marti, S.; Camara, J.; Ciruela, P.; Ardanuy, C.

after.abstract: Introduction: The introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines resulted in a decline in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD). Nevertheless, recent studies report a re-emergence of vaccine-included serotypes. Aim: To describe the recent re-emergence of serotype 14 IPD among adults in Catalonia and to investigate the factors underlying its resurgence. Methods: We analysed two collections of adult IPD isolates: a historical series from Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge (1996-2025) and a multicentre series from seven tertiary hospitals in Catalonia (2023-2025). Isolates were serotyped (Quellung) and genotyped by PFGE/MLST (1996-2022) or Illumina sequencing (2023-2025). Clinical data were retrospectively collected. Results: The historical series showed that, after peaking in 2009, serotype 14 frequency gradually declined, with only -4 cases reported annually between 2016 and 2020. However, the number of serotype 14 isolates increased again in 2025, reaching 11.0% of all isolates at HUB and 10.8% across Catalonia. Genomic data showed that this increase involved multiple previously circulating lineages (GPSC6, GPSC18, GPSC16 and GPSC39), with no dominant clone. Analysis of the capsular locus revealed substantial genetic diversity, with no association between capsular variants and either lineage or year of isolation. A substantial proportion of patients (56.3%) had multiple comorbidities and only 18.8% were appropriately vaccinated. Discussion: The re-emergence of serotype 14 was not associated with a novel lineage or capsular variant. Instead, it may reflect a combination of post-pandemic transmission changes, higher-valency paediatric vaccines, and natural fluctuations in serotype circulation. These findings highlight the limits of herd protection and underscore the need to strengthen adult vaccination, particularly among at-risk populations.

after.authors: Uddin, M. N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Westcliff University
after.abstract: Insurance-related differences in post-acute care after critical illness have mostly been studied within single conditions or settings. We described differences between Medicaid and private insurance in discharge destination and length of stay among working-age adults in two non-equivalent settings: 20,511 patients whose first hospitalization included an ICU stay at one Massachusetts academic medical center (2008 to 2022), and 603,512 Texas hospitalizations with ICU or coronary care unit accommodation charges in 325 acute care hospitals (2017 to 2019). Adjusted for admission-time characteristics, Medicaid was associated in both settings with more skilled nursing facility discharge (5.2 and 4.3 percentage points), less inpatient rehabilitation (-2.0 and -2.6 points), and longer stays. Long-term acute care and total facility use differed in direction. Destination differences persisted with further adjustment and in a common 2017 to 2019 period; length-of-stay differences narrowed. Texas Medicaid rules limiting adult freestanding rehabilitation and inpatient days are consistent with, but cannot establish, a role for benefit design.

after.authors: Komasawa, M.; Sato, M.; Honda, S.; Kitakule, P.; Waiswa, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Nagasaki University School of Tropical Medicine and Global Health
after.abstract: Purpose: Unmarried adolescents in Uganda have limited access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, and conventional programs have struggled to reach them sustainably. Mobile money vendors (MMVs) are ubiquitous in young people's daily lives. We assessed the feasibility of an MMV-based intervention to provide condoms and SRH information to adolescents. Methods: In this type-II hybrid effectiveness-implementation study in Eastern Uganda, 30 MMVs provided oral and printed information, free condoms, and referrals for four months in 2024. Feasibility was assessed using the Bowen framework, drawing on service logs, baseline and endline surveys of adolescents aged 15-19 years (n = 1,204), three focus group discussions with MMVs, eight key informant interviews, a post-intervention MMV survey, and supervision reports. Results: MMVs recorded 104,849 adolescent customer visits; oral information was provided at 54,365 visits and condoms at 21,056 visits. Condom use in the intervention arm increased from 67.3% to 77.7% (p = 0.04), and the proportion obtaining condoms from MMVs rose from 0% to 64.6%. Adolescents valued the service's convenience and confidentiality. Initial resistance from some community adults largely diminished, although referrals remained few (210 cases). All MMV shops completed the intervention without disrupting business, and customer numbers and sales rose 1.64- and 1.50-fold. Suggested adaptations included vendor identification and services for girls, integration with public health systems for scalability. Conclusions: The MMV-based approach was feasible and reached hard-to-access unmarried adolescents with condoms and SRH information. For scale-up, improvements for adaptation and large-scale evaluation are necessary.

after.title: Preprint: Wastewater metagenomic sequencing quantitatively tracks transmission dynamics for human pathogenic viruses
after.authors: Chan, E. M. G.; Justen, L.; Zulli, A.; McLaren, M. R.; Linfield, R. Y.; Moskatel, L. S.; Whittaker, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Division of Infectious Diseases and Vaccinology, School of Public Health, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA
after.abstract: Wastewater metagenomic sequencing theoretically characterizes all nucleic acids in a sample, but whether sequencing reads reflect transmission dynamics of circulating viruses in the contributing community is unknown. We evaluated if wastewater metagenomic sequencing data can be used to reconstruct transmission dynamics of endemic, routinely circulating viruses. Using deep, untargeted wastewater metagenomic sequencing data from four locations in the United States, we generated quantitative estimates of transmission dynamics (time-varying growth rate and effective reproduction number) within a Bayesian framework for widely monitored viruses. Across locations and viruses, estimates were statistically concordant with those derived from clinical surveillance and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based wastewater monitoring data. Furthermore, we estimated growth rate from wastewater metagenomic sequencing data for numerous viruses not otherwise widely monitored, demonstrating the data expands the targets that can feasibly be monitored in parallel. Wastewater metagenomic sequencing can support both novel pathogen detection and routine surveillance of endemic pathogens.

after.title: Preprint: Physical calibration and signal periodic updates to synchronize IMUs for 5-day continuous knee flexion tracking
after.authors: Song, K.; Baxter, J. R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pennsylvania
after.abstract: Wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors provide a promising method to assess real-world human motion kinematics. However, multi-day multi-IMU tracking is difficult due to the desynchronization driven by inaccurate IMU clocks. In this study, 15 volunteers wore IMUs continuously on their thighs and shanks for 5 weekdays (Mon-Fri), which included 3 repeated in-lab motion capture sessions. We synchronized thigh and shank IMUs using two methods. The first was physical calibration, where we maneuvered the IMUs in a rigid holder to produce sync signals pre-donning (Mon) and post-doffing (Fri), then linearly resampled data from one IMU to match the other via cross-correlation. The second was signal-based periodic updates, where we shifted IMU clocks hourly based on the timewise alignment of preprocessed body-worn acceleration signals. After syncing, we used sensor-to-segment alignment and accelerometer-gyroscope fusion to estimate knee flexion and compared results to camera-based motion capture. Physical calibration alone removed clock offset in most cases, where IMU-estimated knee flexion generally matched motion capture (correlation [≥]0.944; root-mean-square difference RMSD [≤]6.9 degrees). But in some participants, residual mid-week desynchronization (~0.2s) resulted in misestimated knee flexion (Wed: RMSD up to ~19 degrees). After applying signal-based updates or combining it with physical calibration, IMU matched motion capture on all 3 days (Mon: r [≥]0.975, RMSD [≤]6.1 degrees; Wed: r [≥]0.971, RMSD [≤]6.2 degrees, Fri: r [≥]0.977; RMSD [≤]5.9 degrees). Our multi-modal synchronization enables week-long knee flexion tracking and lays a foundation for advanced syncing tools, for improving the feasibility of wearable multi-IMU systems to continuously monitor real-world knee kinematics in clinical studies.

after.title: Preprint: Barriers and facilitators to cervical precancer treatment adherence among women in Harare, Zimbabwe: A qualitative study
after.authors: Mutibura, B.; Murewanhema, G.; Chirenje, Z. M.; Mhungu, N.; Guzha, B. T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University Of Zimbabwe
after.abstract: Adherence to recommended treatment after a positive cervical screening result remains suboptimal in Zimbabwe. This study explored how women interpreted a cervical precancer diagnosis and how emotional, interpersonal, economic, and health-system factors shaped treatment decisions. We conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with 25 purposively selected women aged 25-50 years who had screened positive by visual inspection with acetic acid and were recommended for ablative or excisional treatment at two high-volume clinics in Harare. The qualitative component drew on the Health Belief Model and a phenomenological orientation to lived experience. Data were examined using combined deductive and inductive thematic analysis. Three interrelated themes were identified. First, women initially interpreted precancer through fear, shock, and uncertainty; misconceptions that precancer meant invasive cancer, infertility, or imminent death could delay action, whereas clear counselling reframed the diagnosis as treatable. Second, multilevel conditions shaped adherence. Supportive health workers, partner or family encouragement, prior awareness, and connection to HIV services facilitated treatment, while indirect costs, transport, fragmented referral pathways, scheduled excisional services, inconsistent communication, partner opposition, and sexual coercion impeded care. Third, Health Belief Model constructs operated in both directions: perceived severity motivated action when paired with credible benefits and self-efficacy, but produced avoidance when amplified by misinformation and weak support. Improving treatment completion will require standardised counselling, reliable navigation and follow-up, more accessible excisional services, and interventions that address partner dynamics and indirect costs. Screening scale-up should be matched by timely treatment capacity so that women with positive results complete the prevention pathway.

after.authors: Bachu, A.; Rajesh, R.; Ciecierska, S.-S.; Ahn, Y. J.; Germanwala, A. V.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurological Surgery, Loyola University Chicago Stritch School of Medicine, 2160 S. First Avenue, Maywood, IL 60153, United States
after.abstract: Background: Federal small business awards from the National Institutes of Health fund neurosurgical devices and procedural technologies, but how often the specific funded capability reaches human use is unknown. We determined how often these technologies had documented human implementation and in which settings. Methods: We assembled a retrospective public-source cohort of technologies supported by Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer awards from fiscal years 2005-2020 by keyword filtering and funded-purpose review. Confirmation required living-human use of the funded capability or a supported direct extension after a qualifying same-technology award, with public evidence by October 8, 2026. Exploratory comparisons examined program, observed phase, award era, and cumulative support. A 500-family random sample assessed screening omissions. Results: The cohort comprised 209 technologies, 221 award families, and 453 applications receiving $206,825,343. Human implementation was documented for 31/209 technologies (14.8%; Wilson 95% confidence interval, 10.7%-20.3%); evidence was not located for 156 and was indeterminate for 22. Confirmed settings were neurosurgical-scope care (26), other clinical care (2), mixed surgical cohorts (1), and nonclinical human evaluation (2). Confirmation was more frequent with observed Phase II support than Phase I only (21/98 vs 10/111; difference, 12.4 percentage points; company-component bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 2.8-22.4). None of four conventional tests met a Holm-adjusted .05 threshold. Screening scenarios estimated 40-76 omitted families. Conclusion: Approximately one in seven included technologies had documented human implementation. Linking individual awards to implemented capabilities provides an empirical benchmark for early neurosurgical translation and a practical foundation for tracking subsequent clinical evaluation.

after.title: Preprint: Prompt Injection Can Alter Large Language Model Scores and Feedback on Medical Student Essays: A Four-Model Stress Test
after.authors: Cook, D. A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Mayo Clinic College of Medicine and Science
after.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) can support health professions educational assessment by scoring narrative text. However, educator-authored scoring instructions and student text enter the same language-processing context. Prompt injection exploits this boundary by embedding LLM-directed instructions ("attacks") within to-be-assessed text. The scope of this problem across different LLM configurations, attack conditions, and attacker objectives remains incompletely characterized. This study explores: How susceptible is LLM scoring to various prompt injection attacks embedded in reflection essays? Methods: This adversarial stress test examined LLM-based scoring of 4 fabricated medical student reflection essays across 8 prompt injection conditions and 4 LLM configurations. We selected 4 essays used in a previous study representing human reference scores 1 to 4 (maximum 6). In October 2026, we used GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.2, and GPT-6-Luna to score each essay 15 times without modification ("clean") and 5 times for each prompt injection attack. Six "score-targeting attacks" sought the maximum score of 6; 2 "feedback-targeting attacks" sought unauthorized change to narrative feedback, testing whether injections can control the scorer apart from the score itself. The primary outcome was attack success. Results: For clean replications, exact agreement with the human reference standard was 45/60 (75%) for GPT-4.1-mini and >98% for other LLMs. Across all score-targeting attacks and LLMs, 140/480 (29.2%) attained the target score of 6. Analyzed by LLM, 62/120 (51.7%) were successful for GPT-4.1-mini; 51 (42.5%) for GPT-4.1, 25 (20.8%) for GPT-5.2, and 2 (1.7%) for GPT-6-Luna. Analyzed by attack condition, score-targeting success ranged 6% to 56%. Among feedback-targeting attacks, 157/160 achieved success (98.1%), with [≥]95% success for each LLM. Conclusions: Prompt injection is an unresolved threat to LLM-based scoring and feedback. Although score-targeting attacks were often resisted, feedback-targeting attacks were nearly always successful. No LLM was uniformly resistant, and resistance to one attack provided little assurance about another.

after.authors: Takahashi, M.; Kitsuka, N.; Maruoka, H.; Abe, K.; Orimo, S.; Inaba, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Division of Neurology and Gerontoroly, Department of Internal Medicine, Iwate Medical University
after.abstract: Background: Cardiac sympathetic denervation varies in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Our previous neuropathological study demonstrated an association between greater Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and milder cardiac sympathetic denervation in DLB. We investigated whether medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA), a potential marker of concomitant AD pathology, correlates with cardiac sympathetic denervation assessed by 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) cardiac scintigraphy in probable DLB. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, we analyzed 162 patients with probable DLB. MTA was assessed by Voxel-based Specific Regional Analysis System for Alzheimer's Disease (VSRAD) Z-scores, and cardiac MIBG uptake by early and delayed heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios. Associations were examined using Spearman and partial Spearman correlations adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, and disease duration. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with MIBG-dependent classification, diabetes mellitus or cardiac disease. Results: VSRAD Z-scores correlated positively with early ({rho} = 0.173, P = 0.028) and delayed H/M ratios ({rho} = 0.225, P = 0.004). After adjustment, the association was no longer significant for the early H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.133, P = 0.094), whereas it remained significant for the delayed H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.196, P = 0.013). The adjusted delayed H/M association persisted after excluding 18 patients with MIBG-dependent classification ({rho} = 0.211, P = 0.012) and 40 with diabetes or cardiac disease ({rho} = 0.231, P = 0.011). Conclusions: Greater MTA was associated with relatively preserved cardiac MIBG uptake in probable DLB, particularly on delayed imaging. Consistent with our neuropathological observations, these findings suggest that concomitant AD pathology may contribute to variability in cardiac sympathetic denervation.

after.authors: Wiskoski, H. E.; Zahra, S.; French, S. R.; Arias, J. C.; Waughman, X.; Do, L.; Escareno, C.; Vidana, P.; Mushtaq, R.; Johnson, K.; Altbach, M. I.; Reiman, E. M.; Elahi, F. M.; Vitali, F.; Bedrick, E.; Trouard, T. P.; Alexander, G. E.; Weinkauf, C. C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Surgery, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Department of Neuroscience, University of Arizona
after.abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimers Coordinating Center, Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

after.authors: Amrapala, A.; Hemrungrojn, S.; Nupairoj, N.; Solmi, M.; Tunvirachaisakul, C.; Maes, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
after.abstract: Background Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild behavioral impairment (MBI) are overlapping prodromal states associated with dementia risk. Circulating apolipoproteins (Apos) may be linked to cognitive and behavioral changes, but their relationships remain unclear. Objective Examine plasma concentrations of multiple Apos in prodromal dementia. Methods This cross-sectional study included 148 Thai participants aged 60-75 years: 56 cognitively normal controls, 47 with MCI without MBI, and 45 with MBI with or without MCI. We measured ApoA1, ApoA2, ApoB, ApoC1, ApoC3, ApoD, ApoE, ApoH, and ApoJ, five lipids, and APOE genotype, and computed an atherogenic Apo composite (ApoB-ApoC1-ApoC3). Primary analyses used multivariable linear regression of quantitative cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Group comparisons were secondary and served to contextualize the dimensional regression findings. Results Across Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) models, 20.7-28.2% of variance was explained by combinations of ApoH, ApoC3, APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status, age, and male sex (inverse associations), and free cholesterol and education (positive associations). The atherogenic composite was inversely associated with MoCA total, memory index, and delayed recall scores, and with Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) verbal fluency and word list recall. No significant predictors emerged for Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) scores or NPI caregiver distress. All nine Apos differed significantly between groups, with levels highest in MCI, intermediate in MBI, and lowest in controls. Conclusions Circulating Apo profiles differed across controls, MCI, and MBI groups and were more consistently associated with cognitive than behavioral outcomes. ApoH and the atherogenic Apo composite warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of early cognitive dysfunction.

after.authors: Lu, J.; Leech, R.; Snelson, M.; Marques, F.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Monash University
after.abstract: Background & Aims: Dietary fibre is an essential macronutrient for human health. Whether fibre intake has changed in Australia over the last decade remains unknown. This study estimated usual fibre intake among Australian children and adults in 2023 and compared it with 2011-12. Methods: We used data from the 2011-12 (n=12,153) and 2023 (n=11,198) National Nutrition and Physical Activity Surveys with repeat 24-hour recalls. Usual intake was estimated with the National Cancer Institute method and compared with the Adequate Intake (AI) and the Suggested Dietary Target (SDT) levels. Fibre density (g/1,000 kcal) was modelled jointly with energy. Results: Mean usual fibre intake in adults decreased by 2.1 g/day (95% confidence interval 1.6-2.6), from 22.9 to 20.8 g/day. The proportion meeting the AI fell from 24.6% to 17.2%, and SDT from 11.4% to 7.5%. Declines occurred in both sexes and were largest among adults aged 51 years and over. Fibre density fell by 3.2% to 10.7 g/1,000 kcal. Intake in children was stable (19.7 and 20.0 g/day), but only 21.8% of adolescents aged 14-18 years met the AI. In 2023, intake was significantly lower in adults from the most disadvantaged areas and in those with hypertension or obesity. Conclusions: Usual fibre intake among Australian adults declined over the last decade, reflecting both lower energy intake and less fibre-rich food choices. Strategies to improve the availability, affordability, and uptake of fibre-rich foods are needed, particularly for adolescents, older adults, and socioeconomically disadvantaged groups.

after.title: Preprint: Beyond prescription: Determinants of low-dose aspirin adoption and uptake across the pre-eclampsia prevention pathway in Nepal - a qualitative study guided by the COM-B model
after.authors: Harrison, L.; Uprety, S.; Ojha, A.; Rai, T.; Paudel, P.; Dhungana, J.; Chandrasekaran, S.; Ramakrishnan, U.; Shrestha, A.; Rhodes, E. C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Emory University
after.abstract: Despite strong evidence supporting low-dose aspirin (LDA) for preventing pre-eclampsia among women at risk, implementation remains suboptimal globally. The prevention pathway encompasses early antenatal care engagement, screening and risk identification, prescribing LDA, and medication uptake. This qualitative study explored barriers and facilitators to LDA adoption by providers (i.e., prescribing) and uptake among women in Nepal. A qualitative study was conducted with pregnant women, healthcare providers, and maternal and child health stakeholders in Nepal. Data collection and analysis were guided by the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, and Behavior (COM-B) model. Participants were purposively recruited from three tertiary hospitals and maternal health organizations. Semi-structured interviews explored experiences and perspectives related to antenatal care, such as pre-eclampsia risk screening, LDA prescribing, and uptake. Data were analyzed using rapid qualitative analysis and organized according to the COM-B components.   Seventy-three participants were interviewed, including 36 pregnant women, both at risk and not at risk for pre-eclampsia; 29 healthcare providers, including consultant/senior obstetricians, mid-level doctors, and nurses or midwives; and 8 maternal and child health stakeholders representing government, multi-lateral, non-governmental, professional, and academic institutions. LDA adoption and uptake were affected by interdependent gaps across the prevention pathway. Delayed antenatal care engagement and inconsistent screening limited timely identification of women at risk, while gaps in national guidance and standardized prescribing protocols contributed to variable provider prescribing practices. Among women prescribed LDA, clear counselling on its purpose and safety and trust in providers supported uptake. LDA adoption and uptake depend on a functioning prevention pathway in which women engage with antenatal care early enough for timely risk assessment, those at risk are identified through screening, providers prescribe appropriately, and women are supported to use the medication. Strengthening this pathway requires coordinated attention to health-system and provider capacity as well as communication with women, rather than strategies focused narrowly on prescribing or medication use. These findings will inform the development of implementation strategies for Nepal and other low-resource settings seeking to integrate evidence-based preventive interventions into maternal healthcare systems.

after.title: Preprint: Exome-wide rare-variant associations vary across disease trajectories
after.authors: Wang, Y.; Luo, W.; Hu, L.; Chen, T.; Lu, W.; Dowd, C.; Wen, C.; Bi, W.; Koyama, S.; Surakka, I.; Neale, B. M.; Daly, M.; Nataranjan, P.; Martin, A.; Zhou, W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Massachusetts General Hospital; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; Ohio State University
after.abstract: Genetic studies of chronic disease typically collapse longitudinal clinical histories into binary case-control outcomes, obscuring disease timing and differences in genetic association patterns across disease transitions. Time-to-event analysis can preserve this information, but rare-variant analysis of post-diagnosis progression is challenged by sparse carrier-events and extensive censoring. We developed GATE-GENE, a scalable gene-based framework that maintains calibration under these conditions. Across 300 onset phenotypes in UK Biobank (UKB), GATE-GENE identified 107 exome-wide significant germline associations involving 89 genes and 67 diseases. Across 95 multi-state trajectories comprising baseline (T0), an upstream disease state (T1) and a downstream disease state (T2), disease onset (T0[->]T1) and subsequent progression (T1[->]T2) showed limited detectable sharing of rare-variant association signals. Progression showed greater concordance of gene-level association signals with downstream phenotypes (T0[->]T2) when the analyses shared T2 events occurring after T1. Removing overlapping downstream events reduced the median correlation between gene-level association signals from 0.063 to 0.001, after accounting for background correlation. Null simulations reproduced the relationship between event overlap and concordance without genetic effects, whereas additional simulations showed that near-zero concordance could persist despite extensive underlying causal-gene sharing. This attenuation was reproduced across three ancestry groups in All of Us. Cross-biobank meta-analysis identified 12 additional exome-wide significant progression associations beyond three UKB discoveries, although clinical sensitivity analyses suggested that the strongest PKD1 signals largely reflected underlying cystic kidney disease. Together, these findings establish GATE-GENE for investigating rare-variant associations with disease timing and progression, while demonstrating how overlapping clinical events and limited carrier-event information complicate inference about genetic sharing across disease transitions.

after.title: Preprint: Private Equity Practice Connections and Medicare Professional Payments Among US Neurological Surgeons
after.authors: Bachu, A.; Rajesh, R.; Uram, Z.; Chinthala, A.; Germanwala, A. V.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurological Surgery, Loyola University Chicago Stritch School of Medicine, 2160 S. First Avenue, Maywood, IL 60153, United States
after.abstract: Background: Medicare payment patterns among neurosurgeons with private equity connections remain poorly characterized. We compared annual professional payments by connection type. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, public Medicare provider summaries for 2013-2024 were linked to dated affiliation and investment records. The primary comparison included 69 practice or management-services organization-connected surgeons and 4,016 comparison surgeons. Connected surgeons contributed index-year payments; comparison surgeons contributed averages over eligible years. Welch comparisons of log payments estimated geometric mean ratios. Supporting analyses examined dollar differences, state-year standardization, beneficiary age/risk balance, 35 hospital-operator surgeons, and longitudinal trajectories. Payments were expressed in 2024 US dollars. Results: The primary geometric mean ratio was 1.38 (95% confidence interval 1.11-1.72; P = .004). The arithmetic mean difference was +$31,250 (-$3,006 to +$65,506); the state-year standardized difference was +$32,204 (+$2,886 to +$65,372). Age/risk balancing attenuated the ratio to 1.25 (1.01-1.59). The hospital-operator ratio was 0.53 (0.35-0.81); the pooled ratio was 1.00 (0.81-1.25). Among 50 longitudinally eligible practice or management-services organization-connected surgeons, the differential annual change was +16.9% (-0.3% to +37.2%) on the log scale and -$15,727 (wild cluster bootstrap interval -$95,893 to +$35,191) in dollars. Excluding one high-billing surgeon reversed the dollar estimate. All intervals are 95% confidence intervals. Conclusion: Practice and management-services organization connections were associated with higher unadjusted payments; balancing attenuated the ratio to 1.25. Hospital-operator payments were lower. Longitudinal estimates were imprecise and do not establish acquisition effects.

after.title: Preprint: Investigating the Lived Experiences, Needs, and Stories (LENS) of Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome Patients and Caregivers
after.authors: Lynch, G. K.; Hars, E. S.; Cirino, A. L.; Thompson, A. S.; Merker, V. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Massachusetts General Hospital
after.abstract: Background: Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome is a rare genetic condition characterized by pancreatic insufficiency, skeletal differences, and hematologic manifestations. Previous research has focused on describing diagnosis and treatments of the disease. There is a gap in research highlighting SDS patient perspectives. This study aimed to elucidate the challenges of living with and seeking treatment for SDS based on the lived experiences of SDS patients and caregivers. Methods: We conducted semi-structured interviews via Zoom or telephone calls with adults with SDS and caregivers of people with SDS. A semi-structured guide was developed by a multidisciplinary team and utilized for each interview. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed within the Dedoose platform. Three analysts performed inductive open coding of initial transcripts to collaboratively develop a codebook. The final codebook was applied to remaining transcripts by one analyst. Thematic analysis was performed to draw meaning from codes and identify common themes. Results: 20 participants consented and were interviewed for this study, including 11 caregivers of loved ones with SDS and 9 adults with SDS. Two larger themes were identified: 1) SDS Impact on Daily Life and 2) Navigating Healthcare as an SDS Patient or Caregiver. Symptoms and management of SDS affected a wide range of areas, including careers, education, recreational activities, and socialization. When navigating the healthcare system, many participants shared that they felt misunderstood by providers and needed to frequently advocate for themselves or their loved ones. Numerous participants faced issues with accessing specialists who were knowledgeable or willing to learn about SDS and expressed the need for increased patient resources to help navigate a new diagnosis. Conclusions: This study highlights the lived experiences of those impacted by SDS. Participants explained the impact of SDS symptoms and management on all aspects of daily life including career, socialization and extra-curricular activities. Additionally, people expressed that the development and distribution of SDS-specific resources are needed to improve both new patient and healthcare provider education. Increased awareness and education of the condition and the unique medical needs within clinical settings is necessary for expanding access to care.

after.title: Preprint: Efficacy of an early first dose of whole-cell pertussis vaccine in infants for the prevention of IgE-mediated food allergy: A randomised controlled trial
after.authors: Perez Chacon, G.; Totterdell, J.; Estcourt, M. J.; Perrett, K. P.; Campbell, D. E.; Marsh, J. A.; Wood, N.; Bartlett, A. W.; Williams, P. C. M.; O'Sullivan, M. D.; Waddington, C. S.; Messina, N. L.; Wainstein, B.; Hsu, P.; McAlister, S.; Jones, M. A.; Hughes, C.; Wadia, U.; McIntyre, P. B.; Curtis, N.; Gold, M.; Holt, P. G.; Richmond, P. C.; Snelling, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Sydney School of Public Health, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of Sydney, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia.
after.abstract: Background Evidence from mechanistic and observational studies suggests that replacing the first acellular pertussis (aP) vaccine dose in early infancy with a whole-cell pertussis (wP)-containing vaccine may reduce the risk of developing IgE-mediated food allergy during childhood. Objective We aimed to determine if a dose of wP at approximately 6 weeks old, in lieu of aP vaccine, could reduce the incidence of food allergy in infants. Methods In this multicentre, randomised, participant and outcome assessor-blinded, parallel, two-stage, Bayesian adaptive trial we assigned Australian infants to one of two pertussis vaccination schedules. These consisted of either a standard homologous priming with a hexavalent combination aP vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, aP, hepatitis B, inactivated poliovirus types 1, 2, and 3, and Haemophilus influenzae type b; DTaP-HepB-IPV-Hib) at approximately 6 weeks, 4 months and 6 months old ( aP-only&rsquo schedule), or a first dose of a WHO-prequalified pentavalent wP combination vaccine (DTwP-HepB-Hib; Pentabio, PT Bio Farma Indonesia) at approximately 6 weeks old, followed by hexavalent aP combination vaccine at approximately 4 months and 6 months old ( mixed wP/aP&rsquo schedule). The primary outcome was physician-confirmed food allergy by age 12 months requiring both evidence of sensitisation and compatible symptoms in response to either incidental or medically supervised oral food challenge. The initial target sample size was 3,000 enrolments to provide approximately 85% power to detect a policy-relevant 3 percentage point reduction in the risk of the primary outcome. Results A total of 972 infants were enrolled, 486 in each study arm. Of these, 26 of 486 (5.3%) assigned to the aP-only group and 31 of 486 (6.4%) assigned to the mixed wP/aP schedule met the primary endpoint definition. The posterior median difference (95% credible interval) in food allergy among recipients of the mixed wP/aP schedule compared to recipients of the aP-only schedule was 0.01 (-0.02, 0.04; probability [<0] 0.25). There were six serious adverse events (SAEs) among children receiving the aP-only group versus 12 among children receiving the mixed wP/aP schedule; one SAE (hospitalisation for irritability; length of stay < 48 hours) was deemed related to wP vaccine. The trial was stopped early owing to operational reasons. Conclusions There is a low probability of a policy-relevant reduction in food allergy in infants receiving mixed wP/aP versus aP-only pertussis vaccine schedules. Funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia; ANZCTR number, ACTRN12617000065392p. Clinical implications An early first dose of wP is unlikely to afford a policy-relevant reduction in the probability of developing food allergy, eczema or atopic sensitisation in infants. Capsule summary An early first dose of a 5-in-1 wP combination vaccine is reasonably tolerated but would not be expected to have a material impact on the prevalence of food allergy in infants. Key words Diphtheria-Tetanus-Pertussis Vaccine. Diphtheria-Tetanus-acellular Pertussis Vaccines. Food Hypersensitivity. Infant. Australia.

after.title: Preprint: Participant Outcomes of the Diabetes and WELLbeing 12-Week Psychoeducational Self-Management Programme for Type 2 Diabetes: A Four-Country European Evaluation
after.authors: Mukherjee, A.; Shergill, S. S.; Hotham, S.; Vanbosseghem, R.; Gijssel, M.; Manship, S.; Hulbert, S.; Hatzidimitriadou, E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Kent and Medway Medical School, University of Kent
after.abstract: Introduction: Diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) improves glycaemic control, but its benefits often fade once programmes end, and psychosocial outcomes are evaluated less often. We evaluated participant outcomes of the Diabetes and WELLbeing (DWELL) programme, a 12-week psychoeducational self-management programme for adults with type 2 diabetes delivered in four European countries. Methods: In this uncontrolled pre-post evaluation, 605 adults with type 2 diabetes were recruited in the UK, France, Belgium and the Netherlands. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, at programme completion (12 weeks) and at 6-month follow-up. The primary outcome was diabetes self-care (Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities); secondary outcomes included HbA1c, weight, BMI, waist circumference, empowerment, illness perceptions, eating behaviour, health status, physical activity and quality of life. Within-person changes were tested with paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: Of 605 participants, 453 were assessed at programme completion and 293 at 6 months. Most self-care behaviours improved by programme completion (for example, dietary self-care rose from a median of 2 to 3 days per week), and all seven self-care measures differed significantly from baseline at 6 months (r=0.41 to 0.82; all p<0.001). By programme completion, weight (median 1.25 kg), waist circumference (2.0 cm) and HbA1c (2.5 mmol/mol) had fallen, and empowerment, illness coherence, emotional and external eating, physical and mental health and quality of life had improved (all p<0.001). At 6 months, all metabolic outcomes remained below baseline, although HbA1c had partly rebounded (1.7 mmol/mol below baseline), and most psychosocial gains were sustained. Conclusions: Participation in DWELL was associated with improvements in self-care, metabolic and psychosocial outcomes that were partly sustained 6 months after the programme ended. As an uncontrolled evaluation, the study cannot establish causation, and controlled studies with longer follow-up are needed.

after.authors: Oliveira, T.; Reynolds, S. R.; Scanlon, E.; Child, V.; McManus, D. T.; Johnston, B.; Hu, Z.; Killcoyne, S.; Nutzinger, B.; Devonshire, G.; Fitzgerald, R. C.; Turkington, R. C.; McKnight, A. J.; Coleman, H. G.; Curtius, K.
